# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** County Cork was constituted as an administrative county in 1606, making it one of the largest historic counties in Ireland.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Cork City (also spelled Corcaigh in Irish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Munster, Ireland (under British administration as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, from 1801)
- **Population during period:** Population data for the specific 1830–1850 window did not return from the tool query, but County Cork was Ireland's most populous county by the 1841 census, with approximately 854,000 residents. The Great Famine (1845–1852) caused catastrophic loss through death and emigration.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural, with tenant farming, dairying, and fishing. The port of Cobh (then called Queenstown) was a major transatlantic departure point. Butter export through Cork City was significant. Textile manufacturing existed in smaller towns.
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly Irish Catholic, with a Protestant Anglo-Irish landlord class (Church of Ireland). Small Quaker and Presbyterian communities existed in Cork City and some market towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant), Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian, Methodist, and Society of Friends (Quaker).
- **Key historical events:** The 1798 Rebellion aftermath; the Catholic Emancipation Act (1829); the Tithe War (1830–1836), in which tenant farmers resisted paying tithes to the Church of Ireland — directly generating the Tithe Applotment Books; the onset of the Great Famine from 1845, which drove mass emigration from Cork ports.

## Boundary changes

County Cork's external boundaries were stable throughout the 1830s–1840s. Internally, the Poor Law Act of 1838 created Poor Law Unions that cross-cut parish and barony boundaries — these unions administered poor relief and generated their own records. The county was divided into baronies, which were subdivided into civil parishes and then townlands. Church of Ireland civil parishes and Roman Catholic parishes do not align — a civil parish may contain parts of several Catholic parishes, or vice versa. Identifying the correct Catholic parish for a specific townland is essential before searching registers.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Civil registration of births, deaths, and Roman Catholic marriages did NOT begin until 1 January 1864, at the national (Ireland-wide) level. Non-Catholic (principally Church of Ireland) marriages were registered from 1845. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **What exists for 1830s–1840s:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period for Catholic families. Church of Ireland marriages have civil registration from 1845 onward.
- **Where held:** General Register Office of Ireland (GRO), Werburgh Street, Dublin; and the General Register Office of Northern Ireland (GRONI) for records relating to the six counties of Northern Ireland (not applicable to Cork).
- **Gaps:** The entire 1830s–1840s for Catholic families. Church records (below) are the mandatory substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Roman Catholic parish registers; Church of Ireland registers; Quaker and Methodist registers.

### Church records

This is the single most important record category for County Cork in the 1830s–1840s.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant), Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist, Society of Friends.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, and burials. Confirmations are a separate dated event in Catholic registers, usually recorded years after baptism. Catholic registers rarely recorded burials before the mid-19th century; Church of Ireland registers more often did.
- **Roman Catholic registers:** The National Library of Ireland (NLI) holds digitized images of Catholic parish registers up to 1880, freely accessible online at registers.nli.ie. Many Cork Catholic parishes have registers beginning in the 1810s–1830s, though survival is uneven by parish. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Church of Ireland registers:** Held by the Representative Church Body (RCB) Library, Dublin, and in some cases local church custody. The RCB Library has a searchable catalogue online. Note: the 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed many Church of Ireland registers that had been deposited with the Public Record Office — survival varies significantly by parish.
- **Language:** Records are in English (Catholic registers from the 1820s onward are almost entirely in English, though earlier ones may include Latin entries).
- **Critical step:** You must identify the specific Catholic parish and civil parish for the townland where your ancestor lived before searching registers. The townland is the smallest unit of Irish administration. Tools such as the Townlands of Ireland database and the civil registration district maps help connect a townland to its parishes.

### Census records

- **National census:** The Irish census was taken in 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871, 1881, and 1891. However, the 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed nearly all pre-1901 returns. The 1841 and 1851 returns for Cork are almost entirely lost. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **What survives:** Fragments only. The 1821 and 1831 census returns for a small number of Cork parishes survived and are held at the National Archives of Ireland (NAI).
- **Census substitutes (essential for this period):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** List occupiers of tithe-liable agricultural land by townland. Cork's volumes are a central source for the 1830s. Available free online at the NAI website and on Ancestry (indexed). ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
  - **Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork in the early 1850s):** The primary valuation of every householder and land occupier; effectively a census substitute for the late 1840s–early 1850s. Available free online at askaboutireland.ie and on Ancestry (indexed). ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
  - **Poor Law Union records (from 1838):** Workhouse admission and discharge registers, outdoor relief lists, and rate books name ordinary families, including the very poor.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, and estate papers.
- **Date range:** Probate records from before 1858 were handled by the Church of Ireland diocesan courts (Diocese of Cork and Ross, Diocese of Cloyne). From 1858 onward, the Principal Probate Registry in Dublin and district registries handled probate.
- **Record loss:** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the original will books and grant books held at the Public Record Office. What survives is largely indexes and abstracts — the NAI holds the surviving indexes and some transcripts. Burke's Landed Gentry and estate papers in private collections may supplement.
- **Where held:** National Archives of Ireland, Bishop Street, Dublin; some surviving original wills at the NAI or in diocesan archives; indexes are partially online.
- **Note:** Formal probate is more likely for landowners and tradespeople than for poor tenant farmers. Most agricultural laborers in Cork in this period would not have left a will.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ireland used a metes-and-bounds system based on townland, civil parish, barony, and county divisions. The primary land unit for research is the townland.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under the landlord system, most County Cork land was held by Anglo-Irish landlords; tenant farmers held leases. The land was surveyed by the Ordnance Survey in the 1830s–1840s (producing the six-inch maps, freely available online at osi.ie). Estate papers (landlord records) are a significant source for tenant names.
- **Types:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** See Census Substitutes above.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** See Census Substitutes above.
  - **Estate papers:** Rent rolls, lease agreements, and tenant correspondence held in the NAI, the National Library of Ireland, and some private collections. These are largely unindexed and require knowing the landlord's name.
  - **Registry of Deeds (from 1708):** Registered memorials of deeds, wills, and leases, held in Dublin. The indexes are partially online via the Irish Manuscripts Commission.
- **Where held:** NAI (Dublin); NLI (Dublin); Registry of Deeds (Henrietta Street, Dublin).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1798 Rebellion and its aftermath; service in the British Army and Royal Navy throughout the period; the Irish militia. Cork men served in many British regiments.
- **Record types:** British Army service records (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK — series WO); pension records (Royal Hospital Kilmainham pension registers, held at NAI); militia musters; muster rolls for Cork regiments.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (TNA), Kew, UK for British service records; NAI for Irish militia; some records online via Findmypast.
- **Note:** The Cork County militia and the North Cork Militia generated muster rolls and pay lists that name ordinary Cork men who would not appear in church records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Finbarr's Cemetery (Cork City); St. Joseph's Cemetery (Cork City); numerous Church of Ireland churchyards in towns and villages; Roman Catholic burial grounds attached to chapels; unbounded rural burial grounds (cillin) for unbaptized infants.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has some Cork entries but coverage for rural areas in the 1830s–1840s is thin. The Irish Graveyards project and the Cork Archaeological and Historical Society have transcribed some burial grounds.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survived, are held by individual parishes or local archives. The RCB Library holds Church of Ireland burial registers for many Cork parishes.
- **Note:** Most Catholic burials in this period were not formally recorded. A gravestone inscription may be the only surviving evidence. Gravestone Photographic Resource (igp.ie) and Interment.net have some Cork transcriptions.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Cork Examiner (founded 1841 — directly covering the 1840s), the Cork Constitution (established 1822), the Southern Reporter, and the Cork Advertiser were all publishing in this period.
- **Where held:** The British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) holds digitized runs of some Cork papers. The NLI and Cork City Library hold microfilm. The Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com) covers some titles. The Cork Examiner archive from 1841 is partially available.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices (more common for middle-class families), notices of estate sales, legal notices, emigrant ship sailings, and Poor Law announcements. Coverage heavily skewed toward property owners and the professional class.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Cobh (Queenstown), County Cork, was the primary Cork emigration port and a major transatlantic departure point, particularly during and after the Great Famine. Cork City itself also had sailings. Liverpool was a common secondary departure port for those who crossed from Ireland by steamship.
- **Record types:**
  - **Passenger lists (arrival manifests):** US passenger lists record arriving passengers from 1820 onward. Pre-1891 lists are less detailed (name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only). Available on Ancestry (indexed) and at NARA. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
  - **Naturalization records:** Filed at the first US court of record where the immigrant appeared; declarations of intention ("first papers") and petitions for naturalization ("second papers"). Filed in any US federal or state court, so the location depends entirely on where the immigrant settled.
  - **Famine relief ship records:** Some landlord-assisted emigration schemes from Cork in the late 1840s generated passenger lists or estate records identifying the emigrants by name.
  - **UK outward passenger lists:** The Board of Trade (BT series, TNA Kew) recorded departures from British ports from 1890 onward — outside this period, so not directly applicable for 1830s–1840s departures.
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family emigration, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))

### Tax records

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** The most important tax-linked record for the 1830s. Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land by townland throughout County Cork. Available free at the NAI online, and indexed on Ancestry. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Grand Jury Presentments:** County-level taxation and public works records held at Cork county archives. Name ratepayers and sometimes contractors.
- **Poor Rate books:** From 1838, when the Poor Law was introduced, rate collectors recorded every rateable property and occupier. These are among the most comprehensive household listings for the period.
- **Where held:** NAI (Tithe Books); Cork City and County Archives (local rate books and presentments).

### Other record types

- **Ordnance Survey Name Books and Memoirs (1830s):** The Ordnance Survey field officers compiled detailed notes on townlands, naming residents, occupations, religious affiliation, and local history. Partially published; originals at the RIA (Royal Irish Academy) and online via PRONI/Ordnance Survey Ireland.
- **Estate papers:** Many Cork landlord estates deposited their papers at the NLI or NAI. Rent rolls, lease books, and correspondence name tenants who appear in no other source. Locating them requires knowing who owned the land where your ancestor lived.
- **Catholic parish school records:** National school registers from 1831 onward (when the national school system was established) survive for many Cork parishes. Registers name the child, parents, address, and religion. Held at NAI.
- **Poor Law Union workhouse records:** Admission and discharge registers, medical officer reports, and minute books for Cork's Poor Law Unions (Cork, Bandon, Bantry, Clonakilty, Dunmanway, Fermoy, Kanturk, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Midleton, Millstreet, Mitchelstown, Skibbereen, and others) are at the NAI, Cork City and County Archives, and some local repositories.
- **City directories:** For Cork City residents, Pigot's and Slater's commercial directories from the 1820s–1840s list tradespeople and professionals by name, address, and occupation. Available at the NLI and partially digitized.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant for County Cork, 1830s–1840s | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland — registers.nli.ie | Roman Catholic parish registers (baptisms/marriages to 1880) | Free |
| National Archives of Ireland — census.nationalarchives.ie | Tithe Applotment Books, surviving census fragments | Free |
| Askaboutireland.ie | Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s), Ordnance Survey maps | Free |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Irish church records index, some passenger lists | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Tithe Applotment Books (indexed), Griffith's Valuation (indexed), US passenger lists | Subscription |
| Findmypast (findmypast.com) | Irish Catholic registers, Church of Ireland records, some military | Subscription |
| Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com) | Cork newspapers including Cork Examiner from 1841 | Subscription |
| British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) | Cork Constitution and other Cork titles | Subscription |
| Registry of Deeds Index (irishmanuscripts.ie) | Memorial indexes from 1708 | Free (indexes); physical visits for full memorials |

Note: The `external_links_search` tool returned only six generic links (Ancestry census collection, FamilySearch wiki category, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) without Ireland-specific collections for this time window. The Ireland-specific repositories above come from the FamilySearch Wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin | Census fragments, Tithe Books, Poor Law records, wills indexes, estate papers, school registers | In-person; many records online |
| National Library of Ireland (NLI), Dublin | Catholic parish register microfilm/digital; estate papers; newspapers; Ordnance Survey | In-person; registers.nli.ie online |
| Representative Church Body (RCB) Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | In-person; catalogue online at ireland.anglican.org |
| Cork City and County Archives | Local rate books, Poor Law Union records, Grand Jury records, local estate papers | In-person; contact for appointments |
| Cork City Library (Cork Central Library) | Local history collection; Cork newspapers on microfilm | In-person |
| The National Archives (TNA), Kew, UK | British Army service and pension records for Irish soldiers | In-person; many online via Findmypast |
| Royal Irish Academy, Dublin | Ordnance Survey Name Books and Memoirs | In-person; some online |

## Records NOT online

- Most Cork estate papers (rent rolls, lease books identifying specific tenants by townland) — physical only at NAI, NLI, or private collections
- Poor Law Union rate books and workhouse registers — largely physical only at Cork City and County Archives or NAI; some transcribed by local societies
- Grand Jury presentments — physical at Cork archives
- RCB Library Church of Ireland registers for parishes where the originals remain in local church custody rather than being deposited at the RCB Library
- Registry of Deeds original memorials (indexes are online, full texts require physical or paid access)
- Cork City directories (pre-1850) — physical at NLI and Cork City Library; not systematically digitized
- National school registers from 1831 — physical at NAI with no comprehensive online index

## Known record losses

The 1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin destroyed most records held at the Public Record Office of Ireland at that date. This is a documented historical fact. The specific losses relevant to County Cork research in the 1830s–1840s include:

- Nearly all pre-1901 Irish census returns, including the 1831, 1841, and 1851 Cork returns (with minor exceptions)
- Many Church of Ireland parish registers that had been deposited with the Public Record Office (survival of Cork Church of Ireland registers varies by parish; the RCB Library's catalogue shows which parishes' registers survived and what date ranges are held)
- Probate will books and grant books for the ecclesiastical courts (indexes survive but the original wills are largely gone)

Church records held at the NLI (Catholic registers) and the RCB Library (Church of Ireland registers remaining in local custody) were not in the Four Courts and were not affected. Land records (Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation) also survived as they were held elsewhere. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))

The fate of any specific Cork Catholic parish register — whether it survived, how early it begins, what years have gaps — depends on that individual parish and cannot be stated categorically here. Checking the NLI's register catalogue at registers.nli.ie for the specific parish is the required step.

## Research tips

- **Identify the townland first.** Every Irish research strategy begins with pinpointing the townland where the ancestor lived. The townland is smaller than a civil parish or Catholic parish, and connecting it to both parish systems is essential before searching any register. Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books are organized by townland. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Civil and Catholic parishes do not align.** A civil parish (used for Church of Ireland records, the Tithe Books, and census administration) is a different geographic unit from a Catholic parish. One does not map neatly onto the other. Always confirm which Catholic parish served the townland in question — the IreAtlas database (seanruad.com) and the online Townlands of Ireland resource are useful for this.
- **Civil registration began late — do not stop at 1864.** For this period, church registers ARE the vital records. Searching only databases that aggregate post-1864 civil records will find nothing for births or deaths in the 1830s–1840s. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Use the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation as a census pair.** The Tithe Books cover c. 1823–1837 and Griffith's covers c. 1847–1864 (Cork volumes in the early 1850s). Together they bracket the target decade and function as the best census substitutes available. The same family name appearing in the same townland in both is strong evidence of continuity. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Search both the arrival manifests and the naturalization file.** A passenger list (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch) gives the arrival date and port; the naturalization declaration of intention (often filed within a year of arrival) gives the birthplace, sometimes to the townland level, and the date and port of arrival. Together they are the bridge back to County Cork. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))
- **Naming customs.** Irish families in this period commonly named children after grandparents: the eldest son after the paternal grandfather, the second son after the maternal grandfather, the eldest daughter after the paternal grandmother, and so forth. This pattern is a useful guide when a baptismal record gives only the parents' names and you need to trace one generation further back. There is no tool-confirmed source for a specific naming rule beyond this general pattern being widely documented for Ireland; verify against the actual records found.
- **Cobh (Queenstown) as a research asset.** Cobh was a tender port for transatlantic liners and the departure point for enormous numbers of Famine-era Cork emigrants. The Queenstown Story heritage centre and Cobh Museum hold local records and emigration records for the port. Searches should include Liverpool departures as well, since many Cork emigrants crossed to Liverpool first and then sailed onward.
- **Poor Law records as a substitute for the very poor.** The Poor Law system created from 1838 onward generated admission and discharge registers for workhouses, rate books listing every rateable property, and relief lists. For the most impoverished families — who may own no land and appear in neither the Tithe Books nor Griffith's — workhouse records and outdoor relief lists may be the only surviving documentation.
- **Estate papers for tenant identification.** If you can identify the landlord estate where your ancestor's townland was located (using Griffith's Valuation, which names the immediate lessor as well as the occupier), the corresponding estate papers at the NAI or NLI may contain lease books or rent rolls naming the family in years not covered by other records.

---

County Cork in the 1830s–1840s is one of the better-documented Irish counties for this period, but the defining reality is that civil registration had not yet begun, and the 1922 fire destroyed almost all census returns. The research strategy for these years depends on church registers (especially Catholic parish registers, freely available online at registers.nli.ie), the Tithe Applotment Books, and Griffith's Valuation as the three foundational pillars, supplemented by estate papers, Poor Law records, and emigration manifests on both the Irish and the destination-country ends.

The next step would be to identify the specific townland and Catholic parish for your ancestor and then check that parish's register at registers.nli.ie to see what years and record types survive.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761, carved from Hampshire County
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron manufacturing, paper mills, and textile manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Yankee (British-descent New Englanders), with some Dutch-descent families near the New York border
- **Key note:** Berkshire County borders **Columbia County and Rensselaer County, New York** to the west/northwest, and **Bennington County, Vermont** to the north — families near these borders frequently appear in records on *both* sides of the state line.

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**The single most important thing to understand:** Massachusetts recorded vital events **at the town level**, not the county level. There is no county vital register.

- **Before 1841:** Vital events exist *only* in the town clerk's local register. There is no state or county index for 1820–1840. You must identify the specific town first.
- **From 1841 onward:** Massachusetts established the first permanent statewide registration system in 1841, so both a town original *and* a state copy should exist for 1841–1850.
- **Marriage intentions:** These are a *separate* document from the marriage record itself. Per Massachusetts law, they were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, but may also appear in the groom's home town and their current residence — check all locations.

### Where to Look

| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (collection 2061550) — name-indexed | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **FamilySearch: Browse-only digitized Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, Berkshire County, 1761–1850** (image group 004500891, 512 images, not name-indexed) | Free; browse page-by-page |
| **Published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** — printed transcriptions for most Berkshire County towns, widely available at major genealogical libraries | NEHGS, FamilySearch Library, many academic libraries |
| **Town clerks** (original records remain with each town) | In-person or mail request |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | State copies from 1841 onward |

---

## Church Records

Church registers are the **most important supplement** to town clerk records for 1820–1841, before statewide civil registration.

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (dominant, nearly every town), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Dutch Reformed (near the New York border), and some Quaker meetings
- **Record types:** Baptisms (birth surrogates), marriages, burials/deaths, membership rolls
- **Notable gap:** FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume of **Congregational Church Records for Pittsfield, 1791–1850** (image group 004500892, 274 images, 0% indexed)

| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (collection 1921657) — name-indexed | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| Congregational Library and Archives, Boston | In-person or written inquiry |
| Local historical societies | In-person |

---

## Census Records

| Census Year | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1820, 1830, 1840 | All household members tallied by age bracket only (no individual names except head of household) | Use to place the family in a specific town |
| 1850 | **All household members named**, with ages and birthplaces | A major step-change; use birthplaces to redirect searches across state lines |
| 1850 Mortality Schedule | Names individuals who died June 1849–May 1850 | Only federal death source for that window |

All censuses are indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.

---

## Other Key Record Types

### Probate Records
- Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships — frequently name children, spouses, and siblings
- **FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (collection 1678901) — name-indexed, free
- Originals: Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield

### Land Records (Deeds)
- Massachusetts is a metes-and-bounds state; deeds at the county level from 1761 forward
- Originals: **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield**; some available online through the Registry

### Military Records
- War of 1812 veterans living in Berkshire County 1820–1850 will have pension files (which give ages and family details)
- Available on **Fold3** and FamilySearch; originals at NARA and Massachusetts Archives

### Cemetery Records
- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) has crowdsourced headstone transcriptions for many Berkshire County cemeteries
- Sexton records (where they survive) held by towns or local historical societies

### Newspapers
- **Pittsfield Sun** (established 1800) carried marriage notices, death notices, and legal notices
- **Berkshire Athenaeum** (Pittsfield Public Library) holds local newspapers on microfilm
- **Newspapers.com** has some digitized Massachusetts papers (subscription)

---

## Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield** | Original probate files from 1761 |
| **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** | Deeds from 1761 |
| **Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield** (pittsfieldlibrary.org) | Local newspapers, local history, genealogical files |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | State vital records from 1841, militia records |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston** (americanancestors.org) | Largest regional genealogical library; extensive Berkshire County holdings — a top-priority stop |
| **Local historical societies** (Berkshire County Historical Society; town-level societies) | Town histories, manuscript collections, cemetery transcriptions |
| **Individual town clerks** | Original vital records |

---

## Critical Research Tips

1. **Work by town, not by county, for 1820–1840.** Use the 1820 or 1830 census to pin the family to a specific town *first*, then search that town's records.

2. **Start with the printed "Vital Records to 1850" series.** These published transcriptions for most Berkshire County towns are faster than browsing raw volumes and are widely available at NEHGS and major libraries.

3. **Search both sides of the state lines.** If the family was near the New York or Vermont border, vital events, church memberships, probate, and land transactions may appear in **Columbia County, Rensselaer County (NY)**, or **Bennington County (VT)** records. The 1850 census birthplaces for each family member will tell you if any were born across the line, redirecting the search.

4. **The 1850 census is a step-change.** It names every person with age and birthplace — use it to calculate birth years and identify where parents were born (possibly New York or Vermont), which redirects vital-record searches.

5. **Church records are essential for 1820–1841.** Since there was no statewide registration until 1841, Congregational and other church registers are the primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials before that date.

6. **Check NEHGS (americanancestors.org).** It holds the largest genealogical collection in the region and has historically gathered Berkshire County materials not available elsewhere.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761, as a county carved from the western frontier of Hampshire County
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts (state); Hampshire County (predecessor)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this query; the 1820 and 1840 federal censuses are the primary documentary sources for population counts
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron manufacturing (ore deposits in the hills), paper mills, and textile manufacturing, particularly along river valleys
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Yankee (British-descent New Englanders) in this period, with some Dutch-descent families near the New York border and early arrivals from Connecticut and Rhode Island
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant), Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal/Anglican, and Dutch Reformed (near the New York line); Quaker meetings in some towns
- **Key historical events:** The War of 1812 affected regional trade; the opening of the Western Railroad (1839–1841) through Pittsfield linked the county to Boston and Albany and drove demographic change at the end of the period

## Boundary changes

- Berkshire County was formed in 1761 from Hampshire County; all records before that date are under Hampshire County
- The county's boundaries have been stable throughout the 1820–1850 period and have not changed since formation
- The county borders Columbia County, New York to the west and south; Rensselaer County, New York to the northwest; and Bennington County, Vermont to the north — families near these borders frequently appear in records on both sides

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by the Massachusetts General Court as early as 1639, per the FamilySearch Wiki page [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records). In practice, compliance varied by town and clerk, especially in newly settled western Massachusetts towns in the 18th century.
- **Statewide registration:** Massachusetts became the first state to establish a permanent statewide registration system in **1841** (at the state level). Boston was not included until 1850. For 1820–1840, vital events are recorded **only at the town level** — each town clerk kept the register for their town, and there is no county or state index for that window. For 1841–1850, both the town original and a state copy should exist.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, deaths (and marriage intentions, typically recorded in the bride's home town, with additional copies possible in the groom's town and current residence).
- **Where held:** The **original records remain with the town clerk** of each Berkshire County town. Researchers must identify the specific town and contact that clerk, or consult one of the derivative compilations below.
- **The "Vital Records to 1850" published series:** The wiki_search result from [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial) confirms that published compilations titled "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" exist for over 200 Massachusetts towns. These are available at major genealogical libraries (NEHGS, FamilySearch Library) and in many cases have been digitized. They transcribe the town clerk records and are the fastest entry point.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (image group 004500891, 512 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) covering Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records for 1761–1850. This must be browsed image by image with no name search. The indexed statewide FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection 2061550) also covers this county and period and is name-searchable — search it first.
- **Gaps:** Not all Berkshire towns kept complete records before 1841. Marriage intentions are a separate series from the marriage record itself — check both.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist churches are in nearly every town; Methodist and Baptist congregations formed in many towns in the first decades of the 19th century; Episcopal parishes, some Dutch Reformed congregations near the New York border, and small Quaker meetings also operated in the period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (serving as birth surrogates), marriages, burials/deaths, and confirmations (a separate dated event). Some denominations also kept membership rolls and discipline records naming individuals.
- **Where held:** Some registers remain with local congregations; others have been deposited at the Congregational Library and Archives (Boston), the United Methodist Archives (Madison, NJ), or local historical societies. FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (image group 004500892, 274 images, 0% indexed) of Congregational Church Records for Pittsfield, Berkshire County, covering 1791–1850. The statewide FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (collection 1921657) is name-indexed.
- **Language:** English throughout this period for Berkshire County churches.
- **Critical note:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial records are the most important source for vital events in 1820–1841, before statewide civil registration, and remain a significant supplement after 1841. If your family's specific town has incomplete town clerk records, church registers are the primary fallback.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Available for 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850. The 1850 census is the first to name all household members individually (with ages and birthplaces) rather than tallying by age bracket.
- **Mortality schedules:** Beginning with 1850, the mortality schedule names individuals who died in the year preceding the census (June 1, 1849 – May 31, 1850), making it the only federal source for deaths in that final census year.
- **State census:** Massachusetts did not take a regular state census between federal censuses in this period. The federal census is the only enumeration for most years.
- **Access:** The 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses for Berkshire County are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations (intestate), inventories, guardianships, and estate distributions. These frequently reveal family relationships — children's names, spouses, and sometimes siblings.
- **Date range:** Berkshire County Probate Court records run from the county's formation in 1761 (earlier deaths were handled by Hampshire County). The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (collection 1678901) is indexed.
- **Where held:** The Berkshire County Probate Court in Pittsfield holds the original records. The FamilySearch Catalog may have microfilm copies; check the catalog directly at FamilySearch.org for Berkshire County probate.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is an original-colony, state-land state — no federal land grants).
- **Types:** Deeds recorded at the county Register of Deeds from the county's formation in 1761. Land transfers name grantor and grantee, often with neighbors and family members as witnesses.
- **Where held:** The Berkshire County Registry of Deeds in Pittsfield holds the originals. The wiki_search result notes that Massachusetts land records "survive in remarkably complete runs" from the 1630s (source: [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The War of 1812 (1812–1815) falls within or just before the period; service records and pension files for veterans living in Berkshire County in 1820–1850 are at the National Archives.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (which often give ages and family details), bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, DC and Waltham, MA regional branch); military pension files are heavily indexed on Fold3 and FamilySearch.
- **State records:** The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds state militia records and some adjutant general records for the period.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Every Berkshire County town has at least one burying ground, often associated with a Congregational church or established as a town cemetery by the early 19th century.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) provides crowdsourced headstone transcriptions and photographs for many Berkshire County cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they exist, are typically held by the town or local historical society.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Pittsfield was home to newspapers throughout the period, including the Pittsfield Sun (established 1800). These carried marriage notices, death notices, and legal notices (estate settlements, land sales).
- **Where held:** The Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield Public Library) holds the primary collection of local newspapers on microfilm. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) provides digitized access to some Massachusetts newspapers with subscription.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and marriage notices often provide information not recorded in official registers, particularly for the 1820–1841 window before statewide civil registration.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** Berkshire County is far inland. International immigration to the county in 1820–1850 was limited, but domestic migration — families moving from Connecticut, Rhode Island, and older Massachusetts counties, or emigrating west to New York and Ohio — was common.
- **Record types:** The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312) covers coastal arrivals, not directly relevant to most Berkshire County families in this period.
- **Naturalization:** The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906" (collection 1459213) covers any foreign-born residents who naturalized through Massachusetts courts, including Berkshire County courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) name every person aboard, including infants traveling with parents. When researching immigrant families, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town and county tax assessment lists exist for most of the period.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can document a person's presence in a town in years between censuses, and can serve as substitutes when vital or census records are missing.
- **Where held:** Originals at the individual town clerks or Massachusetts Archives; some have been transcribed or microfilmed.

### Other record types

- **Published town histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published histories of Berkshire County towns often include genealogical appendices listing founding families, sometimes the only surviving transcription of records since lost.
- **The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS):** Per the wiki_search result from [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military), NEHGS holds the largest genealogical library in the region and has extensive Berkshire County holdings.

### Physical repositories

| Town clerks (each Berkshire County town) | Original vital records — births, marriages, deaths, and marriage intentions | In-person or mail request; fees vary by town |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Original probate files from 1761 onward | In-person or written request |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deeds from 1761 onward | In-person; some records available online through the Registry |

| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston (https://www.americanancestors.org) | Largest regional genealogical library; extensive Massachusetts holdings including Berkshire County | In-person; online database by subscription |
| Congregational Library and Archives, Boston | Congregational church registers | In-person; written inquiry |
| Local historical societies (Berkshire County Historical Society, Pittsfield; town-level societies) | Town histories, manuscript collections, cemetery transcriptions | In-person; hours vary |

## Records NOT online

- Town clerk original vital records for individual Berkshire County towns for 1820–1850 may exist only at the town clerk's office if not captured in the statewide FamilySearch collection or the published "Vital Records to 1850" series
- Tax assessment lists for most Berkshire County towns
- Most local church registers beyond the Pittsfield Congregational browse-only volume at FamilySearch
- Town meeting records and selectmen's records (which can name residents in poor relief lists, road maintenance assignments, and town business)
- Sexton records for individual cemeteries

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey identifies a specific courthouse fire or documented loss of Berkshire County vital, probate, or land records. The FamilySearch catalog and volume search returned results suggesting survivorship of the town clerk and probate series. The absence of a loss report is a coverage gap in the survey, not proof of complete survival — contact the holding repositories directly to confirm the condition of specific series.

## Research tips

- **Work by town, not by county, for vital records before 1841.** Massachusetts registered vital events at the town level from 1639 onward; there is no county vital register. You must know which town (or narrow it to two or three candidates) before searching. The 1820 and 1830 censuses will place a household in a specific town. (Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records))
- **Search both the bride's and groom's home towns for marriage intentions.** Per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page, marriage intentions were "commonly recorded in the bride's home town and additional recordings may be found in the groom's home town and their current residence." A marriage intention is a separate document from the marriage record itself — it may survive even when the marriage record does not. (Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records))
- **The statewide series begins in 1841 — not earlier.** For births, marriages, and deaths in 1820–1840, the only official record is the town clerk's local register. State-level indexes do not cover that window. (Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records))
- **Use the published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series as your starting point.** These printed transcriptions cover most Berkshire County towns, are widely available in major genealogical libraries, and are faster to consult than browsing the raw town clerk volumes. (Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial))
- **Search across the New York and Vermont state lines.** Berkshire County borders Columbia County and Rensselaer County in New York, and Bennington County in Vermont. A family living near the line — particularly a town like Adams, Williamstown, Lanesborough, or Alford — may have used churches, courts, or stores on the other side. New York recorded vital events at the town level as well; Vermont at the town level. Searching only Berkshire County records for a border-town family risks missing events filed under Columbia, Rensselaer, or Bennington counties. The specific neighboring towns within those counties are not returned by the tools used in this survey — consult a historical atlas to identify them for your specific town.
- **The 1850 census is a step change in information.** Unlike 1820, 1830, and 1840, the 1850 federal census names every person in the household with age and birthplace. If your family is present in 1850, it gives exact ages that you can use to calculate birth years, and birthplaces for each individual — including parents born in New York or Vermont, which would redirect the vital-record search across the border.
- **Check NEHGS (americanancestors.org) for unique Berkshire County holdings.** The New England Historic Genealogical Society holds the largest genealogical library in the region and has historically collected Berkshire County manuscript materials not available elsewhere. (Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military))

---

For a family researching births, marriages, and deaths in Berkshire County, Massachusetts between 1820 and 1850, the most important thing to understand is that vital events in this period were recorded at the town level, not the county level, and there was no statewide registration until 1841. That means you must first pin the family to a specific town using the 1820 or 1830 census, then search that town's clerk records — either through the printed "Vital Records to 1850" series available at major genealogical libraries, or through FamilySearch's indexed statewide collection and its browse-only digitized volume for the county. Church records (especially Congregational) are the most important backup when town records are thin, and the family's proximity to the New York and Vermont borders means events may appear in Columbia County, Rensselaer County, or Bennington County records as well.

Once you have confirmed the specific town, the next step is to search that town's vital records in the FamilySearch collection (collection 2061550, free) and check whether a published "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" volume exists for that specific town.

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **County:** Antrim, province of Ulster
- **Barony:** Dunluce Lower
- **County seat:** Antrim town; **Provincial capital:** Belfast
- **Sovereign jurisdiction:** Parliament of Ireland until 1800; United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1801 onward

- **Religious composition:** Heavily Ulster Scots (Presbyterian); also Church of Ireland (Anglican) and a smaller Roman Catholic population — a legacy of the 17th-century Ulster Plantation
- **Key events:** 1798 United Irish Rebellion; Acts of Union 1800; Great Famine 1845–1852 (major emigration spike); sustained emigration to North America throughout the period

---

## Boundary Changes

- Billy is an ancient Church of Ireland civil parish whose boundaries were essentially stable throughout 1780–1870.
- From 1821, civil parishes served as the base unit for census enumeration.
- Under the Poor Law Act (Ireland) 1838, Billy parish was placed within the **Ballymoney Poor Law Union**; Poor Law records are therefore held at the union level.
- No subdivision or merger of the Billy civil parish occurred within the target period.

---

## Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

| Coverage | Date |
|---|---|
| Non-Catholic marriages only | From 1 April 1845 |
| All births, marriages, and deaths (all denominations) | From 1 January 1864 |

For **1780–1863** — the bulk of the target window — there are **no civil vital records** for Billy parish. Church registers are the only substitute. Civil registration covers only the final 6 years (1864–1870) of the target window.

**Where held:** General Register Office (GRO), Roscommon (originals); PRONI, Belfast (Northern Ireland copies); indexes free online at **IrishGenealogy.ie**.

**Gaps:** The entire pre-1864 period has no civil birth, death, or burial records; pre-1845 has no civil marriage records whatsoever.

---

### Church Records

North Antrim was heavily **Presbyterian**, so identifying the correct denomination for a given family is the first priority — do not default to Church of Ireland registers.

**Denominations present:** Church of Ireland (Anglican), Presbyterian (multiple congregations in the Bushmills area), Roman Catholic, Methodist, Reformed Presbyterian (Covenanting).

**Record types:** Baptism/christening registers, marriage registers, burial/death registers, vestry minutes (Church of Ireland), session minutes and communion rolls (Presbyterian).

**Where held:**

| Denomination | Primary repository | Online access |
|---|---|---|
| Church of Ireland | PRONI, Belfast; RCB Library, Dublin | IrishGenealogy.ie (some registers) |
| Presbyterian | PRONI, Belfast; Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast | Limited |
| Roman Catholic | With local parish / Diocese of Down and Connor; microfilm at PRONI and NLI | **registers.nli.ie** (free, browse by parish) |

Specific register survival for individual Billy parish congregations could not be confirmed from tool output. Confirm holdings directly with PRONI and the relevant denominational archives before planning a visit.

---

### Census Records

Irish national census years within the target period: **1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871.**

- The **1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851** returns for most of Ireland were destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire** in Dublin. County Antrim (including Billy parish) has **no surviving national census** for these years.
- The **1861 and 1871** returns were destroyed by government order.
- This means there is effectively **no surviving national census for Billy parish within the target period**.

**Census substitutes are critical:**

| Substitute | Approximate date | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | c. 1823–1837 | Landholders (not labourers or cottiers) | Free at NAI online; also FindMyPast |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | c. 1856–1858 (Antrim) | All land and property occupiers | Free at **AskAboutIreland.ie** |
| 1796 Flax Growers' List | 1796 | Those who received spinning wheels | Ancestry and some free databases |
| 1901 and 1911 census (postdate target period) | 1901, 1911 | All household members | Free at **census.nationalarchives.ie** |

---

### Probate and Court Records

**Before 1858 (ecclesiastical courts):** The Consistorial Court of Down and Connor held probate jurisdiction for ordinary County Antrim estates. The Prerogative Court of Armagh handled larger estates. The vast majority of pre-1858 Irish will books and administration bonds were **destroyed in 1922**. Surviving fragments include Sir William Betham's abstracts (at NAI) and printed indexes.

**From 1858 onward (civil system):** The District Probate Registry served the Belfast district; PRONI holds these records. Annual printed **Will Calendars** from 1858 survived the fire and are available at PRONI, NAI, and partly online.

---

### Land Records

Billy parish is organized into townlands (sub-units of the civil parish). Land records are organized at the townland level.

| Record | Dates | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1796 Flax Growers' List | 1796 | Ancestry; some free databases |
| Tithe Applotment Books | c. 1823–1837 | Free at NAI; FindMyPast |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | c. 1856–1858 | Free at AskAboutIreland.ie |
| Registry of Deeds (deeds, mortgages, leases) | From 1708 | Indexed; originals at Registry of Deeds, Dublin |
| Estate papers (landlord rentals, lease books) | Various | PRONI, Belfast (in-person / by appointment) |

**Estate papers** for north Antrim landlords at PRONI can name individual tenants and are especially valuable for the years 1780–1820, when no census or valuation substitutes exist.

---

### Military Records

**Relevant conflicts:** 1798 United Irish Rebellion; Napoleonic Wars (British Army and militia service).

**Record types and where held:**
- British Army service records and pension records → The National Archives, Kew (England); many digitized at FindMyPast and Ancestry
- Irish Militia muster rolls → NAI and PRONI (some)

---

### Cemetery Records

Church of Ireland and Presbyterian graveyards attached to churches within Billy parish, plus Roman Catholic burial grounds.

**Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have volunteer-submitted inscriptions; coverage for specific Billy parish graveyards is unconfirmed from tool output. The **Ulster Historical Foundation** and local north Antrim historical societies have conducted gravestone surveys for County Antrim.

---

### Newspaper Records

| Paper | Dates | Coverage area |
|---|---|---|
| Belfast Newsletter | From 1737 | All of Ulster |
| Northern Whig | From 1821 | Ulster |
| Coleraine Chronicle | From 1844 | North Antrim coast |

**Access:** British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk), Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com), Newspapers.com, and Belfast Central Library (microfilm).

**Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, auction notices, legal notices, emigration advertisements — all useful for Billy parish families.

---

### Immigration and Emigration Records

County Antrim had significant emigration throughout 1780–1870, accelerating sharply after the Famine (post-1845). Principal departure ports: Larne and Belfast. Principal destination ports: Philadelphia, New York, Baltimore, Quebec, and Saint John.

**Record types:**

- Pre-1820 passenger lists are fragmentary; newspaper notices are the main source
- Canadian arrivals → Library and Archives Canada

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Key collections for Billy parish | Access |
|---|---|---|
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil registration (births from 1864, marriages from 1845/1864, deaths from 1864); some Church of Ireland registers | **Free** |
| AskAboutIreland.ie | Griffith's Primary Valuation (fully indexed) | **Free** |
| NAI / census.nationalarchives.ie | Tithe Applotment Books; 1901 and 1911 census; school records | **Free** |
| registers.nli.ie | Roman Catholic parish registers (browse by parish) | **Free** |
| PRONI online (proni.gov.uk) | Index to church registers; some civil registration for Northern Ireland | Free index; some images in-person only |
| FindMyPast | Tithe Applotment Books; British newspaper archive; some Irish church records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Griffith's Valuation; U.S. passenger lists; some Irish church records | Subscription |
| FamilySearch | Some Irish church records and civil registration indexes | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Key holdings |
|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** (proni.gov.uk) | Church registers (microfilm and originals); estate papers; Poor Law (Ballymoney Union) records; civil registration; census substitutes |
| **National Archives of Ireland, Dublin** (nationalarchives.ie) | Pre-1922 records; will abstracts; Tithe Books; valuation records; school registers |
| **General Register Office, Roscommon** | Original civil registration records from 1845/1864 |
| **Representative Church Body Library, Dublin** | Church of Ireland registers and vestry records |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast** | Presbyterian session records and registers |
| **Diocese of Down and Connor Archives** | Roman Catholic registers and diocesan records |
| **The National Archives, Kew** | British Army records; some plantation-era Irish records |
| **Ballymoney Library** | Local newspapers; north Antrim local history collections |

---

## Known Record Losses

**1922 Four Courts fire (Dublin):** The most significant loss in Irish genealogy. Destroyed:
- Irish census returns for **1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851** — no comprehensive substitute census survives for County Antrim
- Most pre-1858 **will books and administration bonds** from ecclesiastical courts, including the Consistorial Court of Down and Connor

**1861 and 1871 census returns:** Destroyed by government order — not a fire loss, but a deliberate destruction.

**Key point:** The 1922 fire is not a total loss. Many indexes, abstracts, transcripts, and microfilm copies made before 1922 survive at PRONI, NAI, and other repositories. Always check for secondary copies before concluding a record is gone.

---

## Irish Naming Conventions (from the FamilySearch Wiki)

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ireland Naming Customs" — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Naming_Customs*

- Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were anglicized under English rule. The prefixes *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson/descendant of) were frequently dropped or restored — so the same family may appear as **O'Flynn, Flynn, and Flinn** across different records. Spelling was not standardized; multiple spellings within a single register are common.
- Some Gaelic given names were anglicized into seemingly unrelated English names (e.g., Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah can all represent the same Gaelic name).
- Some given names were used for both sexes (e.g., Florence, Sydney, Evelyn).
- A **traditional naming pattern** was commonly followed until the later 19th century:

| Child | Typically named for |
|---|---|
| First son | Father's father |
| Second son | Mother's father |
| Third son | Father himself |
| Fourth son | Father's eldest brother |
| First daughter | Mother's mother |
| Second daughter | Father's mother |
| Third daughter | Mother herself |

> **The Wiki's own caution:** "The pattern is a clue, not a rule — it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity."

Always try surname variants systematically when searching databases (e.g., search Flynn *and* O'Flynn *and* Flinn).

---

## Recommended Research Sequence for Billy Parish, 1780–1870

1. **Griffith's Valuation (c. 1856–1858)** at AskAboutIreland.ie — free, fully indexed; gives the townland location of every household head in Billy parish at mid-century. Note the townland — all subsequent searches should filter to that townland.

2. **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837)** at NAI or FindMyPast — identifies the same families two to three decades earlier and confirms landholder status in the early part of the target window.

3. **Church registers via PRONI and IrishGenealogy.ie** — first identify which congregation served your family's townland. In heavily Presbyterian north Antrim, many families will appear *only* in Presbyterian registers, not Church of Ireland.

4. **1901 and 1911 censuses** (census.nationalarchives.ie) — anchor the family at the end of the period and work backward; these fully survived and are fully indexed free online.

5. **1796 Flax Growers' List** — useful for identifying households at the very start of the target window (1780s–1790s).

6. **U.S. and Canadian passenger lists** (FamilySearch, Ancestry) — search for emigrant family members, especially post-1845 Famine emigration. Examine the full manifest for all household members.

7. **PRONI estate papers** for the relevant landlord — rental lists and lease books can name individual tenants by townland, especially for 1780–1820 when no census or valuation substitutes exist.

8. **Probate** — search Betham's will abstracts at NAI and the printed Will Calendars from 1858 at PRONI for any testators.

9. **Townlands.ie** — use this free mapping tool to verify the boundaries of Billy parish and identify adjacent civil parishes whose registers should also be searched for families living near a boundary.

---

## Summary

Billy civil parish is a small Church of Ireland civil parish on the north Antrim coast. For 1780–1870, the most important facts to internalize are:

- **No civil vital records exist before 1864** (or 1845 for non-Catholic marriages) — church registers are the primary source for the great majority of this window.
- **No national census survives for any year in the target period** — Griffith's Valuation (1856–1858) and the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) are the essential household substitutes.
- **North Antrim was heavily Presbyterian** — identify the correct denomination before searching registers; do not assume Church of Ireland records cover your family.
- **The 1922 fire is serious but not total** — secondary copies of many destroyed records survive; always check indexes and abstracts before assuming a record is gone.
- **PRONI in Belfast** is the single most important physical repository for Billy parish records.

The recommended first step is to locate the family in Griffith's Valuation to establish their townland, then identify the correct church congregation and confirm whether its registers survive at PRONI.

  - British Army service records and pension records (held at The National Archives, Kew, England; many on FindMyPast and Ancestry).
  - Militia muster rolls for the Irish Militia (some at NAI and PRONI).
  - Irish Memorial Records for World War I (outside this period but relevant for descendants).
- No specific military collection for Billy parish was returned by tools in this session.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Church of Ireland and Presbyterian graveyards attached to the churches in Billy parish (including Bushmills area). Roman Catholic burial grounds in the parish.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has volunteer-submitted headstone inscriptions; coverage for Billy parish graveyards is unconfirmed from tool output. The Ulster Historical Foundation and local historical societies have conducted gravestone surveys in County Antrim.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, vestry burial registers (Church of Ireland), and session records (Presbyterian) may survive at PRONI or with the individual churches.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Coleraine Chronicle* (from 1844) and *Ballymena Observer* (from 1855) are the closest papers to Billy parish in the target period. The *Belfast Newsletter* (from 1737) is the major Ulster paper covering the whole period. The *Northern Whig* (from 1821) is another Belfast paper.
- **Where held:** Belfast Central Library holds microfilm of many Ulster newspapers. The British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) has digitized many Ulster titles; Newspapers.com and the Irish Newspaper Archives (irishnewsarchive.com) also hold some titles.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, auction notices, legal notices, and emigration advertisements — all useful for Billy parish families.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** County Antrim had significant emigration throughout 1780–1870, particularly to North America. The port of Larne and the port of Belfast were major departure points. Emigration accelerated sharply after the Great Famine (post-1845).
- **Relevant ports of entry:** Philadelphia, New York, Baltimore, and Canadian ports (Quebec, Saint John) received most Ulster emigrants.
- **Record types:**
  - Passenger lists for arrivals in the United States (from 1820 for U.S. ports; available at Ancestry and FamilySearch).
  - Pre-1820 passenger lists are fragmentary; some survive in newspaper notices.
  - Naturalization records (filed in any U.S. court of record; pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered).
  - Canadian arrival records (available through Library and Archives Canada).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Hearth Money Rolls (pre-1780; some survive for Antrim), flax growers' premium lists (1796; names those who received spinning wheels — a useful pre-Tithe substitute), Tithe Applotment Books (as above, c. 1823–1837).
- **Date range:** The 1796 Flax Growers' List is particularly useful for the earliest part of the target period and is available online through various Irish genealogy databases.
- **Substitute value:** In the absence of surviving census returns for 1780–1851, the Tithe Books and Griffith's Valuation are the principal substitutes for locating households in Billy parish.

### Other record types

- **Poor Law Union records:** Billy parish is in the Ballymoney Poor Law Union. Records include workhouse admission registers and relief lists (held at PRONI). These document the poorest residents, many of whom are invisible in land-based records.
- **School records:** National School (primary school) registers from the 1830s onward, held at NAI. Some have been microfilmed.
- **Church vestry minutes:** Church of Ireland vestry minutes (at PRONI) can name rate-payers and local office-holders, supplementing land records.
- **Town histories and published genealogies:** Several histories of north Antrim and the Dunluce barony area have been published. The Ballymoney library and local Ulster historical societies hold collections.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
