entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** One of the original Thirteen Colonies; declared an independent commonwealth in 1776
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond became the capital in 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown Colony of Virginia (pre-1776); independent Commonwealth thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for this specific window; the first federal census (1790) counted approximately 747,000 residents, placing the 1775-1783 population somewhat below that figure
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming, milling, iron-working, and coastal/river trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers; significant enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German communities in the western counties; remaining Indigenous communities in interior regions
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (established church through the Revolution; reorganized as Episcopal); Presbyterian; Baptist; Quaker; Lutheran and German Reformed in the Valley
- **Key historical events:** Virginia declared independence from Britain in June 1776; the Virginia Convention drafted one of the first state constitutions; major campaigns included the Southern Theater actions of 1780-1781 and the decisive Siege of Yorktown (October 1781)

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's western boundary was contested and expansive during this period; Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776, and the District of Kentucky was organized from it in 1780
- New county formations were frequent throughout the Revolutionary period as settlement expanded westward
- Records for any given locality follow the county that existed at the time of the event; always determine which county held jurisdiction at the event date before searching

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775-1783. Statewide registration did not begin until 1853 (births and deaths) and lapsed again 1896-1912. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page was not returned by this survey's tool calls; confirm the precise registration history directly at the Library of Virginia.
- **What exists for this period:** No civil birth or death registers. Marriage bonds and minister's returns were recorded at the county level beginning in the colonial period; these are the primary marriage sources for 1775-1783.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond; many are included in FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal vestry books (baptisms, marriages, burials); Presbyterian session minutes; Quaker meeting records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church); Presbyterian; Baptist; Quaker; Lutheran; German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes, poor-relief lists
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives, local parishes, Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) covers the period
- **Language:** English; some German-language records in the Valley counties
- **Note:** Vestry books of the Anglican church are among the best pre-civil-registration vital sources; the established church was disestablished during the Revolution, which disrupted some record-keeping in the late 1770s-1780s

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790; it postdates the target period and the Virginia schedules were destroyed in 1814
- **State tax lists as substitute:** Virginia conducted personal property tax enumerations beginning in 1782. These are the principal population-level substitute for the missing 1790 census and cover the tail end of the war period. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations / tax lists 1782-1799 (imageGroup 005301449; full-text searchable, not name-indexed — browse-only via image)
- **Access:** The tax list volume must be browsed image by image; full-text search is available but not name-indexing. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) also covers post-1782 lists.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War, 1775-1783
- **Record types and locations:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — NARA, Record Group 93; many are accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
  - **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond; these are separate from the federal series
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA, Record Group 15; these files are among the richest genealogical sources for the period, frequently containing affidavits that name wives, children, neighbors, and witnesses. Searchable via Fold3 and Ancestry.
  - **Virginia State Navy records** — published separately; Library of Virginia holds the originals
  - **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) — digitized, indexed
- **Post-war bounty lands:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia and the Ohio Historical Society connect veterans to their claims; these records often survive when other service documentation does not.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianship bonds, estate inventories, appraisements, county court order books
- **Holding level:** County level; circuit court for equity
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia holds many on microfilm; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285) and "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
- **County court order books:** These books record all county business — road assignments, poor-relief payments, orphan bindings, and militia appointments — and name ordinary residents who appear in no military or vital record. A digitized volume of Augusta County court order books (1775-1795) is available on FamilySearch (imageGroup 005301448; 61% name-indexed).
- **Note on wartime wills:** Men going to war often executed wills. Wartime wills and estate proceedings for men who died in service are especially common in this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; the Commonwealth, not the federal government, granted land)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Virginia; grants and patents are held at the Library of Virginia
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deed books, surveyors' plats, bounty warrants
- **Bounty land warrants:** Virginia issued warrants for lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio as payment for Revolutionary War service; these are distinct from federal bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** County deed books at the county courthouse; Library of Virginia for patents and warrants; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285) covers deeds and patents
- **Date range:** County deed books predate the Revolution; patents in Virginia begin in the colonial period

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists), land tax
- **Date range:** Virginia's personal property tax lists begin 1782 — immediately following the target period — and are the single most important substitute for the missing 1790 census
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (collection 1456723 and browse-only imageGroup 005301449)
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 federal census is missing for Virginia, the 1782-1787 tax lists effectively function as a census substitute for the immediate post-war generation of heads of household

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Anglican/Episcopal churchyards were the primary burial sites; family cemeteries on farmsteads are common throughout Virginia
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Virginia churchyard and family cemetery inscriptions
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive from this period; headstone inscriptions are often the only evidence
- **Note:** Many 18th-century markers have weathered beyond legibility; transcription projects by the DAR and local genealogical societies have preserved some readings

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the principal paper during the Revolution; multiple competing editions were published under that name
- **Content value:** Military appointments, notices of deserters, estate administrator notices, and wartime proclamations all appear
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries some digitized Virginia colonial papers

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** During 1775-1783, outbound emigration (Loyalist departures) and inbound migration from other colonies were both occurring; formal passenger manifests are uncommon for this period and for Virginia's many small coastal landings
- **Relevant record types:** Loyalist claims filed in Britain (held at The National Archives, Kew, series AO 12 and AO 13) document families who left Virginia during or after the war; naturalization records are less relevant for this period since most residents were native-born colonists

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** County court minutes record oaths of allegiance; those who refused were sometimes named in court order books. Confiscated Loyalist property records are held at the Library of Virginia.
- **Orderly books and unit records:** Many Virginia regimental orderly books have been published or microfilmed; they name soldiers present and record courts martial
- **DAR and SAR lineage records:** Both organizations hold lineage papers that document Virginia Revolutionary War ancestors; DAR's online database (dar.org) is searchable
- **Published county histories:** 19th-century Virginia county histories (e.g., works by Wayland, Chalkley, and Summers for the Valley counties) often reprint early records and list founding families
- **Daughters of the American Revolution transcription projects:** The DAR transcribed many Virginia court and church records in the early 20th century; these volumes are at the DAR Library in Washington, D.C., and in many genealogical libraries

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (collection 1945678); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (1734285); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1598230); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records (NARA RG 93), pension files (NARA RG 15) | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Ancestry | Pension files, passenger lists, published Virginia genealogies | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions statewide | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Record Group 93 (service records), Record Group 15 (pensions and bounty-land warrants) | Free to search; some documents require in-person or paid copy request (https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 3 digitized volumes matching this place and period; all 3 are detailed above. `collections_search` returned 5 indexed collections (all 5 detailed). This is the complete returned set for both queries.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; land patents and grants; bounty land warrants; county deed and will books on microfilm; state personal property tax lists | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some microfilm loan via interlibrary loan |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington D.C. / College Park | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15); federal census schedules | In-person; mail request; Fold3/Ancestry digital access for many series |
| County courthouses | Deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds — originals held at the courthouse of the county in existence at the time | In-person or written request to each county |
| DAR Library, Washington D.C. | DAR lineage papers; transcribed Virginia records; published genealogies | In-person; partial online access via dar.org |
| Virginia Historical Society (Virginia Museum of History and Culture), Richmond | Manuscript collections, family papers, published local histories | In-person; vamhc.org |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette files; colonial-era manuscripts | In-person; research library |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized or indexed online
- County court order books outside Augusta County are largely browse-only on FamilySearch or not yet digitized
- Loyalist claims records (The National Archives, Kew, AO 12/AO 13 series)
- Most regimental orderly books survive only in physical repositories or published transcriptions
- Vestry books of many individual parishes have not been digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census schedules for Virginia were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; there is no recovery — the 1782-1787 tax lists are the accepted substitute
- This survey's tools did not return specific information about individual county or parish record losses in Virginia for this period; the Library of Virginia and county courthouse staff are the authoritative sources for losses affecting specific counties

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA RG 15) are one of the most genealogically detailed record classes for this era. They frequently include widow's declarations with maiden name, marriage date and place, children's names, and witnesses who knew the family. Search via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) or Ancestry.
- **Use tax lists as a census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census is destroyed, the 1782-1787 personal property tax lists (available at the Library of Virginia and partially on FamilySearch) are the standard substitute for locating heads of household in the immediate post-war period.
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia service.** A man may appear in Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia, in Continental Line records at NARA, or in both — the two series are held at different repositories and neither is a complete substitute for the other.
- **Check bounty land warrants even for non-Ohio researchers.** Virginia's bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio document service even when the veteran never claimed or settled the land; the warrant record alone confirms service.
- **County court order books are underused.** These books record road assignments, orphan bindings, poor-relief, and militia appointments — all naming ordinary residents. The Augusta County order books (1775-1795) are 61% name-indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroup 005301448).
- **Vestry books fill the vital-records gap.** Before and during the Revolutionary period there was no civil registration; Anglican/Episcopal vestry books recording baptisms, marriages, and burials are the primary substitute. Check both the original vestry books and the DAR transcription volumes.
- **Virginia wiki pages returned only generic content** in this survey run. For jurisdiction-specific research guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy and the Library of Virginia's research guides at lva.virginia.gov.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** One of the original Thirteen Colonies; declared an independent commonwealth in 1776
- **County seat / administrative center:** Williamsburg (colonial capital); Richmond became the capital in 1780
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Crown Colony of Virginia (pre-1776); independent Commonwealth thereafter
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the survey tools for this specific window; the first federal census (1790) counted approximately 747,000 residents, placing the 1775-1783 population somewhat below that figure
- **Economy:** Tobacco planting, subsistence farming, milling, iron-working, and coastal/river trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English-descended settlers; significant enslaved African population; Scots-Irish and German communities in the western counties; remaining Indigenous communities in interior regions
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (established church through the Revolution; reorganized as Episcopal); Presbyterian; Baptist; Quaker; Lutheran and German Reformed in the Valley
- **Key historical events:** Virginia declared independence from Britain in June 1776; the Virginia Convention drafted one of the first state constitutions; major campaigns included the Southern Theater actions of 1780-1781 and the decisive Siege of Yorktown (October 1781)

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's western boundary was contested and expansive during this period; Kentucky County was created from Fincastle County in 1776, and the District of Kentucky was organized from it in 1780
- New county formations were frequent throughout the Revolutionary period as settlement expanded westward
- Records for any given locality follow the county that existed at the time of the event; always determine which county held jurisdiction at the event date before searching

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths during 1775-1783. Statewide registration did not begin until 1853 (births and deaths) and lapsed again 1896-1912. The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page was not returned by this survey's tool calls; confirm the precise registration history directly at the Library of Virginia.
- **What exists for this period:** No civil birth or death registers. Marriage bonds and minister's returns were recorded at the county level beginning in the colonial period; these are the primary marriage sources for 1775-1783.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and the Library of Virginia, Richmond; many are included in FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal vestry books (baptisms, marriages, burials); Presbyterian session minutes; Quaker meeting records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church); Presbyterian; Baptist; Quaker; Lutheran; German Reformed
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes, poor-relief lists
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives, local parishes, Library of Virginia; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (collection 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) covers the period
- **Language:** English; some German-language records in the Valley counties
- **Note:** Vestry books of the Anglican church are among the best pre-civil-registration vital sources; the established church was disestablished during the Revolution, which disrupted some record-keeping in the late 1770s-1780s

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was 1790; it postdates the target period and the Virginia schedules were destroyed in 1814
- **State tax lists as substitute:** Virginia conducted personal property tax enumerations beginning in 1782. These are the principal population-level substitute for the missing 1790 census and cover the tail end of the war period. FamilySearch has a digitized volume of Virginia state enumerations / tax lists 1782-1799 (imageGroup 005301449; full-text searchable, not name-indexed — browse-only via image)
- **Access:** The tax list volume must be browsed image by image; full-text search is available but not name-indexing. FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (collection 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) also covers post-1782 lists.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War, 1775-1783
- **Record types and locations:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls** — NARA, Record Group 93; many are accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)
  - **Virginia militia records** — Library of Virginia, Richmond; these are separate from the federal series
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA, Record Group 15; these files are among the richest genealogical sources for the period, frequently containing affidavits that name wives, children, neighbors, and witnesses. Searchable via Fold3 and Ancestry.
  - **Virginia State Navy records** — published separately; Library of Virginia holds the originals
  - **FamilySearch collection:** "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (collection 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) — digitized, indexed
- **Post-war bounty lands:** Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. Warrant and survey records at the Library of Virginia and the Ohio Historical Society connect veterans to their claims; these records often survive when other service documentation does not.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianship bonds, estate inventories, appraisements, county court order books
- **Holding level:** County level; circuit court for equity
- **Where held:** County courthouses; Library of Virginia holds many on microfilm; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285) and "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (collection 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
- **County court order books:** These books record all county business — road assignments, poor-relief payments, orphan bindings, and militia appointments — and name ordinary residents who appear in no military or vital record. A digitized volume of Augusta County court order books (1775-1795) is available on FamilySearch (imageGroup 005301448; 61% name-indexed).
- **Note on wartime wills:** Men going to war often executed wills. Wartime wills and estate proceedings for men who died in service are especially common in this period.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state; the Commonwealth, not the federal government, granted land)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Virginia; grants and patents are held at the Library of Virginia
- **Types:** Land grants/patents, deed books, surveyors' plats, bounty warrants
- **Bounty land warrants:** Virginia issued warrants for lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio as payment for Revolutionary War service; these are distinct from federal bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** County deed books at the county courthouse; Library of Virginia for patents and warrants; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (collection 1734285) covers deeds and patents
- **Date range:** County deed books predate the Revolution; patents in Virginia begin in the colonial period

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists), land tax
- **Date range:** Virginia's personal property tax lists begin 1782 — immediately following the target period — and are the single most important substitute for the missing 1790 census
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch (collection 1456723 and browse-only imageGroup 005301449)
- **Substitute value:** Because the 1790 federal census is missing for Virginia, the 1782-1787 tax lists effectively function as a census substitute for the immediate post-war generation of heads of household

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Anglican/Episcopal churchyards were the primary burial sites; family cemeteries on farmsteads are common throughout Virginia
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Virginia churchyard and family cemetery inscriptions
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rarely survive from this period; headstone inscriptions are often the only evidence
- **Note:** Many 18th-century markers have weathered beyond legibility; transcription projects by the DAR and local genealogical societies have preserved some readings

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) was the principal paper during the Revolution; multiple competing editions were published under that name
- **Content value:** Military appointments, notices of deserters, estate administrator notices, and wartime proclamations all appear
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation; Library of Virginia; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) carries some digitized Virginia colonial papers

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** During 1775-1783, outbound emigration (Loyalist departures) and inbound migration from other colonies were both occurring; formal passenger manifests are uncommon for this period and for Virginia's many small coastal landings
- **Relevant record types:** Loyalist claims filed in Britain (held at The National Archives, Kew, series AO 12 and AO 13) document families who left Virginia during or after the war; naturalization records are less relevant for this period since most residents were native-born colonists

### Other record types
- **Loyalist records:** County court minutes record oaths of allegiance; those who refused were sometimes named in court order books. Confiscated Loyalist property records are held at the Library of Virginia.
- **Orderly books and unit records:** Many Virginia regimental orderly books have been published or microfilmed; they name soldiers present and record courts martial
- **DAR and SAR lineage records:** Both organizations hold lineage papers that document Virginia Revolutionary War ancestors; DAR's online database (dar.org) is searchable
- **Published county histories:** 19th-century Virginia county histories (e.g., works by Wayland, Chalkley, and Summers for the Valley counties) often reprint early records and list founding families
- **Daughters of the American Revolution transcription projects:** The DAR transcribed many Virginia court and church records in the early 20th century; these volumes are at the DAR Library in Washington, D.C., and in many genealogical libraries

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (collection 1945678); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (1734285); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (1598230); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (1456723); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (2134567) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records (NARA RG 93), pension files (NARA RG 15) | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Ancestry | Pension files, passenger lists, published Virginia genealogies | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions statewide | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Record Group 93 (service records), Record Group 15 (pensions and bounty-land warrants) | Free to search; some documents require in-person or paid copy request (https://www.archives.gov/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 3 digitized volumes matching this place and period; all 3 are detailed above. `collections_search` returned 5 indexed collections (all 5 detailed). This is the complete returned set for both queries.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; land patents and grants; bounty land warrants; county deed and will books on microfilm; state personal property tax lists | In-person; online catalog at lva.virginia.gov; some microfilm loan via interlibrary loan |
| National Archives (NARA), Washington D.C. / College Park | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension and bounty-land warrant files (RG 15); federal census schedules | In-person; mail request; Fold3/Ancestry digital access for many series |
| County courthouses | Deed books, will books, court order books, marriage bonds — originals held at the courthouse of the county in existence at the time | In-person or written request to each county |
| DAR Library, Washington D.C. | DAR lineage papers; transcribed Virginia records; published genealogies | In-person; partial online access via dar.org |
| Virginia Historical Society (Virginia Museum of History and Culture), Richmond | Manuscript collections, family papers, published local histories | In-person; vamhc.org |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette files; colonial-era manuscripts | In-person; research library |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully digitized or indexed online
- County court order books outside Augusta County are largely browse-only on FamilySearch or not yet digitized
- Loyalist claims records (The National Archives, Kew, AO 12/AO 13 series)
- Most regimental orderly books survive only in physical repositories or published transcriptions
- Vestry books of many individual parishes have not been digitized

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census schedules for Virginia were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; there is no recovery — the 1782-1787 tax lists are the accepted substitute
- This survey's tools did not return specific information about individual county or parish record losses in Virginia for this period; the Library of Virginia and county courthouse staff are the authoritative sources for losses affecting specific counties

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA RG 15) are one of the most genealogically detailed record classes for this era. They frequently include widow's declarations with maiden name, marriage date and place, children's names, and witnesses who knew the family. Search via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) or Ancestry.
- **Use tax lists as a census substitute.** Because the 1790 Virginia census is destroyed, the 1782-1787 personal property tax lists (available at the Library of Virginia and partially on FamilySearch) are the standard substitute for locating heads of household in the immediate post-war period.
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia service.** A man may appear in Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia, in Continental Line records at NARA, or in both — the two series are held at different repositories and neither is a complete substitute for the other.
- **Check bounty land warrants even for non-Ohio researchers.** Virginia's bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio document service even when the veteran never claimed or settled the land; the warrant record alone confirms service.
- **County court order books are underused.** These books record road assignments, orphan bindings, poor-relief, and militia appointments — all naming ordinary residents. The Augusta County order books (1775-1795) are 61% name-indexed on FamilySearch (imageGroup 005301448).
- **Vestry books fill the vital-records gap.** Before and during the Revolutionary period there was no civil registration; Anglican/Episcopal vestry books recording baptisms, marriages, and burials are the primary substitute. Check both the original vestry books and the DAR transcription volumes.
- **Virginia wiki pages returned only generic content** in this survey run. For jurisdiction-specific research guidance, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy and the Library of Virginia's research guides at lva.virginia.gov.
- **The wiki_search result** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War) is the most specific returned source for Virginia Revolutionary War military record guidance in this survey.

---

**New Orleans, Louisiana — Early 1800s: Record Survival & Substitutes**

New Orleans in the early 1800s was shaped by French founding, Spanish colonial rule, the Louisiana Purchase (1803), and statehood (1812). Two catastrophic fires in **1788 and 1794** destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. However, significant records *did* survive or were copied:

### What Survived the Fires

1. **St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers** — Run from **1731** (with gaps). These baptism, marriage, and burial registers are among the most important surviving colonial records and are often the only source for vital events of free persons of color, enslaved individuals, and Catholics of all backgrounds.

2. **New Orleans Notarial Archives** — Hold over **30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 onward**. Because Louisiana follows the **Napoleonic civil-law tradition**, notarial acts — not deed books as in other U.S. states — document land transfers, wills, contracts, manumissions, and more. One FamilySearch-digitized volume covering **1803–1820 notarial acts** (image group 004990115, 167 images, in French and English) must be browsed image by image since it is not name-indexed.

---

### Key Indexed FamilySearch Collections

- **Louisiana Church Records, 1718–1925**
- **Louisiana Probate Records, 1756–1984** *(called "successions" and "tutorships" — Napoleonic terminology)*
- **Louisiana Statewide Death Index from 1819**
- **Louisiana Parish Marriages from 1837**
- **Federal Censuses from 1810 onward** *(Louisiana was not U.S. territory in 1800, so no 1800 census)*

---

### Where to Look for Copies & Substitutes

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — for the vast majority of notarial holdings not yet digitized; contact in person or by correspondence.
- **Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)** — for state-level civil records and other surviving colonial and early statehood documents.
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — [Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) is the recommended next stop for confirmed vital-records start dates and record-set coverage.

---

### Terminology Notes (Napoleonic Law)
- **Wills/Estates** → called *successions*
- **Guardianships** → called *tutorships*
- **Land & contracts** → documented in *notarial acts*, not deed books

---

**Recommended next step:** Build a research plan targeting specific ancestors using the church records collection and the Notarial Archives — the `research-plan` skill can do this using the locality entry (loc_001) now saved to your project.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Founded:** 1718 by France
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (coterminous with Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Territory of Orleans (1804-1812), then State of Louisiana (1812-present)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this place and period; the city grew rapidly through the antebellum era as a major port. Wikipedia notes New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. cities by 1840.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trade, shipping, warehousing; a major gateway for Mississippi River trade
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American (post-Louisiana Purchase), free people of color, enslaved African and African-descended people, Irish and German immigrants arriving by the 1830s-1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral served the city from 1731), with Protestant congregations arriving after the Louisiana Purchase
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics; hurricanes; fires of 1788 and 1794 (which pre-date the target period but directly affect colonial-era record survival)

## Boundary changes
- **1718-1763:** French colonial territory
- **1763-1800:** Spanish colonial rule (Cabildo government; notarial system formalized)
- **1800-1803:** Briefly returned to France
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase — New Orleans passed to the United States
- **1804-1812:** Territory of Orleans — records created under territorial government
- **1812-present:** State of Louisiana

Records created before 1812 will be under the Territory of Orleans heading, not "Louisiana." Search both headings in catalogs and indexes. Records before 1803 were created under Spanish or French colonial authority.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records resolved to generic content in this survey and did not state a start date or registration level. The Louisiana State Archives (https://www.sos.la.gov/HistoricalResources/ResearchALouisianaAncestor/Pages/default.aspx) should be consulted directly for the civil registration start date and the level (parish vs. statewide) at which registration applied during 1800-1850.
- **What exists:** No statewide civil registration system is confirmed for the early 1800s from tool results. The Louisiana Statewide Death Index (FamilySearch collection 1543892) begins in 1819 and covers through 1964 — it is an index only, with no images.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge. FamilySearch collection 1543892 for the death index (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892).
- **Gaps:** Civil registration was not uniformly required in early Louisiana; fires, floods, and epidemics caused additional losses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary, from 1718); Protestant congregations established after 1803
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — at St. Louis Cathedral from 1731, with gaps caused by fires (1788, 1794) and floods
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed Louisiana church records spanning 1718-1925 (collection 1612905: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905). This collection contains 987,654 records and 493,827 images and is name-indexed.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for pre-1803 and early-post-Purchase records; English increasingly after statehood
- **Note:** The wiki_search result returned by this survey states that sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral survive from 1731 with gaps (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). These are the single most important source for vital events in the early 1800s when civil registration was absent or incomplete.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was included in the federal census from 1810 onward (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 all fall within the target period). The 1800 census does not include Louisiana (not yet a U.S. territory at census time).
- **State/territorial census:** Spanish colonial censuses exist for pre-1803 New Orleans; the FamilySearch Wiki pages did not return Louisiana-specific census guidance in this survey.
- **Access:** Federal census years for Louisiana are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free), Ancestry (subscription at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/), and other platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana civil-law terminology:** In Louisiana's Napoleonic Code-based system, probate records are called "successions" (testate — with a will) and "administrations" (intestate — without a will). Guardianships are called "tutorships." Search these terms specifically.
- **Types:** Successions (wills/testaments), intestate administrations, tutorships (guardianships), inventories, estate distributions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984) covers this period: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 — 456,789 records, 228,394 images, name-indexed.
- **Where held:** Civil District Court, Orleans Parish (succession records); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot (arpent) system in older settled areas, not the U.S. rectangular survey system used in federal-land states
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 Spanish and French land grants were confirmed (or rejected) by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners after the Louisiana Purchase. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Land and Property resolved to generic content in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for confirmation.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (the primary legal instrument for land, contracts, and donations); Spanish and French colonial land grants; U.S. land patents; tax records
- **Most important repository:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). FamilySearch has 1 digitized but unindexed volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts (1803-1820), imageGroupNumber 004990115, in French and English — 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.
- **Date range:** Notarial records from 1734; U.S.-era records from 1803

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815); War of 1812; Louisiana militia service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls, bounty land warrants (for War of 1812 veterans)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 (subscription) — https://www.fold3.com/; Louisiana State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 — all Catholic and in operation during the target period
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave — https://www.findagrave.com/ (many New Orleans cemeteries indexed)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for the St. Louis Cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Multiple French- and English-language papers existed in New Orleans by the early 1800s (e.g., the Louisiana Gazette / New Orleans Gazette, the Louisiana Courier)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com/ (subscription); New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection; Tulane University
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale announcements, sheriff's sale notices (useful for economic distress), runaway slave advertisements, legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. ports of entry — passenger arrival lists are a major source
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA); declarations of intention and naturalizations (filed in various courts, pre-1906); alien registrations
- **Where held:** NARA — https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger list collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (Louisiana parish-level); personal property tax
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish assessor's records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and establish presence in the city

### Notarial records (Louisiana-specific)
- **This is a Louisiana-unique record type** central to all legal transactions under the civil-law system — wills, contracts, land sales, donations, marriage contracts, manumissions, and business agreements were all executed before a notary and retained permanently in the notarial archives.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages from 1734)
- **FamilySearch digitization:** 1 volume, imageGroupNumber 004990115, 167 images, covering 1803-1820 notarial acts — browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable), in French and English

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (1543892); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (DGS 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, federal records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans/Louisiana in the 1800-1850 window — this is consistent across all record-type queries run, suggesting very limited digitization of local volumes at FamilySearch for this place and period. The total for each query was 1, with no nextPageToken, so the result set appears complete for FamilySearch's digitized holdings. The primary indexed collections are at the state (Louisiana) level, not the New Orleans city level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person research; contact for remote inquiries |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records, successions, land records | In-person / online request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Church sacramental registers, school records | Contact for access |
| Civil District Court, Orleans Parish | Succession (probate) records | In-person / court request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Collection | Local histories, newspapers, city directories | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Local histories, plantation records, newspapers | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts (the great bulk of the 30+ million pages at the Notarial Archives Research Center) — physical only
- Most pre-1837 marriage records not captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Original Orleans Parish succession/probate case files beyond what collection 2078341 covers
- City directories and local histories
- Most sacramental registers beyond what FamilySearch's church records collection microfilmed
- Yellow fever death registers and epidemic burial records
- Spanish colonial census records

## Known record losses
- **Fires of 1788 and 1794:** New Orleans suffered two major fires under Spanish rule that destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Per the Wikipedia article on Orleans Parish (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orleans_Parish,_Louisiana) and the wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), these fires caused significant record loss. However, no tool result in this survey confirmed the specific fate of any individual parish register or notarial volume — that determination requires direct contact with the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans.
- **Surviving series despite fires:** The wiki_search result states that sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731) survive with gaps, and that the New Orleans Notarial Archives holds records from 1734 — meaning some records predate and survived the fires. Do not assume all pre-1795 records were destroyed without checking the specific series at its holding repository.
- **Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods:** Per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans), repeated disasters caused additional archival damage. Which specific record sets were affected is not confirmed by tool results — report to repositories for confirmation.
- **Substitute sources for fire-period gaps:** Notarial acts (contracts, wills, manumissions, land transactions), surviving sacramental registers, Spanish colonial census records, and post-fire re-registrations with civil authorities.

## Research tips
- **Understand the civil-law system.** Louisiana is the only U.S. state with a civil-law (Napoleonic Code) tradition. Probate records are called successions; guardianships are called tutorships; legal transactions go through notaries rather than common-law deeds. The FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System confirms this.
- **Notarial records are the research backbone.** Because all legal transactions — land, wills, contracts, donations, manumissions — were executed before a notary, the Notarial Archives Research Center is the first stop for any legal or property question about a New Orleans ancestor. The center holds 30+ million pages from 1734 (per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Do not assume fire destroyed everything.** The 1788 and 1794 fires were catastrophic but some series survived. Always check the holding repository before concluding a record is lost.
- **Church records substitute for absent civil registration.** St. Louis Cathedral records (from 1731 with gaps) are the primary vital-event source before civil registration was established. FamilySearch collection 1612905 is the starting point.
- **Account for multiple languages.** Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early post-Purchase records mix French, Spanish, and English. The 1 digitized FamilySearch notarial volume (DGS 004990115) is in both French and English.
- **The 1800 federal census does not include Louisiana** — it was not yet U.S. territory. The first federal census covering New Orleans is 1810.
- **Search across the territorial/statehood boundary.** Records 1804-1812 are under the Territory of Orleans; records 1812 forward are under the State of Louisiana. Catalogs and indexes may split them — search both headings.
- **Use city directories and newspapers** for the intercensal years — New Orleans had active newspapers from the early 1800s, and city directories appear by the 1820s-1830s. These place people at specific addresses between decennial censuses.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana did not return Louisiana-specific content** in this survey (all resolved to a generic page). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for current research guidance on vital records start dates, census availability, and land records.
- **Neighboring parishes:** New Orleans / Orleans Parish is bordered by Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (east/southeast), and St. Tammany Parish (north across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near these borders may have generated records in those parishes as well. The neighboring parishes were not listed in a wiki-returned table in this survey — confirm adjacencies before broadening the search.

- **Federal census:** Louisiana was included in the federal census from 1810 onward (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 all fall within the target period). The 1800 census does not include Louisiana (not yet a U.S. territory at census time).
- **State/territorial census:** Spanish colonial censuses exist for pre-1803 New Orleans; the FamilySearch Wiki pages did not return Louisiana-specific census guidance in this survey.
- **Access:** Federal census years for Louisiana are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free), Ancestry (subscription at https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/), and other platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana civil-law terminology:** In Louisiana's Napoleonic Code-based system, probate records are called "successions" (testate — with a will) and "administrations" (intestate — without a will). Guardianships are called "tutorships." Search these terms specifically.
- **Types:** Successions (wills/testaments), intestate administrations, tutorships (guardianships), inventories, estate distributions
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984) covers this period: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341 — 456,789 records, 228,394 images, name-indexed.
- **Where held:** Civil District Court, Orleans Parish (succession records); Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge; New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French long-lot (arpent) system in older settled areas, not the U.S. rectangular survey system used in federal-land states
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pre-1803 Spanish and French land grants were confirmed (or rejected) by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners after the Louisiana Purchase. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Land and Property resolved to generic content in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for confirmation.
- **Types:** Notarial acts (the primary legal instrument for land, contracts, and donations); Spanish and French colonial land grants; U.S. land patents; tax records
- **Most important repository:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters). FamilySearch has 1 digitized but unindexed volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts (1803-1820), imageGroupNumber 004990115, in French and English — 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image.
- **Date range:** Notarial records from 1734; U.S.-era records from 1803

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815); War of 1812; Louisiana militia service
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, muster rolls, bounty land warrants (for War of 1812 veterans)
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) — https://www.archives.gov/; Fold3 (subscription) — https://www.fold3.com/; Louisiana State Archives for state militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (est. 1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 — all Catholic and in operation during the target period
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave — https://www.findagrave.com/ (many New Orleans cemeteries indexed)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for the St. Louis Cemeteries are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Multiple French- and English-language papers existed in New Orleans by the early 1800s (e.g., the Louisiana Gazette / New Orleans Gazette, the Louisiana Courier)
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com/ (subscription); New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Collection; Tulane University
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate sale announcements, sheriff's sale notices (useful for economic distress), runaway slave advertisements, legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New Orleans was one of the largest U.S. ports of entry — passenger arrival lists are a major source
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA); declarations of intention and naturalizations (filed in various courts, pre-1906); alien registrations
- **Where held:** NARA — https://www.archives.gov/; Ancestry.com passenger list collections
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax (Louisiana parish-level); personal property tax
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish assessor's records
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years and establish presence in the city

### Notarial records (Louisiana-specific)
- **This is a Louisiana-unique record type** central to all legal transactions under the civil-law system — wills, contracts, land sales, donations, marriage contracts, manumissions, and business agreements were all executed before a notary and retained permanently in the notarial archives.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages from 1734)
- **FamilySearch digitization:** 1 volume, imageGroupNumber 004990115, 167 images, covering 1803-1820 notarial acts — browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable), in French and English

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (1798054); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (2078341); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (1543892); 1 browse-only notarial acts volume (DGS 004990115) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, federal records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** Volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Orleans/Louisiana in the 1800-1850 window — this is consistent across all record-type queries run, suggesting very limited digitization of local volumes at FamilySearch for this place and period. The total for each query was 1, with no nextPageToken, so the result set appears complete for FamilySearch's digitized holdings. The primary indexed collections are at the state (Louisiana) level, not the New Orleans city level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person research; contact for remote inquiries |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records, successions, land records | In-person / online request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Church sacramental registers, school records | Contact for access |
| Civil District Court, Orleans Parish | Succession (probate) records | In-person / court request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Collection | Local histories, newspapers, city directories | In-person |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Local histories, plantation records, newspapers | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana | In-person / online request |

## Records NOT online
- Most notarial acts (the great bulk of the 30+ million pages at the Notarial Archives Research Center) — physical only
- Most pre-1837 marriage records not captured in FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Original Orleans Parish succession/probate case files beyond what collection 2078341 covers
- City directories and local histories
- Most sacramental registers beyond what FamilySearch's church records collection microfilmed
- Yellow fever death registers and epidemic burial records
- Spanish colonial census records

## Known record losses
- **Fires of 1788 and 1794:** New Orleans suffered two major fires under Spanish rule that destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Per the Wikipedia article on Orleans Parish (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orleans_Parish,_Louisiana) and the wiki_search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters), these fires caused significant record loss. However, no tool result in this survey confirmed the specific fate of any individual parish register or notarial volume — that determination requires direct contact with the New Orleans Notarial Archives and the Archdiocese of New Orleans.
- **Surviving series despite fires:** The wiki_search result states that sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731) survive with gaps, and that the New Orleans Notarial Archives holds records from 1734 — meaning some records predate and survived the fires. Do not assume all pre-1795 records were destroyed without checking the specific series at its holding repository.
- **Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods:** Per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans), repeated disasters caused additional archival damage. Which specific record sets were affected is not confirmed by tool results — report to repositories for confirmation.
- **Substitute sources for fire-period gaps:** Notarial acts (contracts, wills, manumissions, land transactions), surviving sacramental registers, Spanish colonial census records, and post-fire re-registrations with civil authorities.

## Research tips
- **Understand the civil-law system.** Louisiana is the only U.S. state with a civil-law (Napoleonic Code) tradition. Probate records are called successions; guardianships are called tutorships; legal transactions go through notaries rather than common-law deeds. The FamilySearch wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System confirms this.
- **Notarial records are the research backbone.** Because all legal transactions — land, wills, contracts, donations, manumissions — were executed before a notary, the Notarial Archives Research Center is the first stop for any legal or property question about a New Orleans ancestor. The center holds 30+ million pages from 1734 (per wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- **Do not assume fire destroyed everything.** The 1788 and 1794 fires were catastrophic but some series survived. Always check the holding repository before concluding a record is lost.
- **Church records substitute for absent civil registration.** St. Louis Cathedral records (from 1731 with gaps) are the primary vital-event source before civil registration was established. FamilySearch collection 1612905 is the starting point.
- **Account for multiple languages.** Records before 1803 are in French or Spanish; early post-Purchase records mix French, Spanish, and English. The 1 digitized FamilySearch notarial volume (DGS 004990115) is in both French and English.
- **The 1800 federal census does not include Louisiana** — it was not yet U.S. territory. The first federal census covering New Orleans is 1810.
- **Search across the territorial/statehood boundary.** Records 1804-1812 are under the Territory of Orleans; records 1812 forward are under the State of Louisiana. Catalogs and indexes may split them — search both headings.
- **Use city directories and newspapers** for the intercensal years — New Orleans had active newspapers from the early 1800s, and city directories appear by the 1820s-1830s. These place people at specific addresses between decennial censuses.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana did not return Louisiana-specific content** in this survey (all resolved to a generic page). Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for current research guidance on vital records start dates, census availability, and land records.
- **Neighboring parishes:** New Orleans / Orleans Parish is bordered by Jefferson Parish (west), St. Bernard Parish (east/southeast), and St. Tammany Parish (north across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near these borders may have generated records in those parishes as well. The neighboring parishes were not listed in a wiki-returned table in this survey — confirm adjacencies before broadening the search.

Here is what the locality-guide agent found for tracing immigrants who arrived in Boston in the 1840s:

---

**Boston, Massachusetts — Immigrant Arrival Records, 1840s**

Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of immigrants — the majority Irish fleeing the Great Famine after 1845, along with smaller British, German, and Canadian communities.

### Key Record Types & Repositories

1. **Port of Boston Customs Passenger Lists**
   - Held at the **National Archives at Boston** (Waltham, Massachusetts)
   - Partially available on **FamilySearch** (collection 1784312) and **Ancestry**
   - *Caveat:* 1840s lists record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not detailed hometown data that later manifests provide.

2. **Naturalization Records**
   - FamilySearch collection **1459213**
   - Before 1906, declarations of intention could be filed in *any* court (Suffolk County, state court, or even courts in other states if the immigrant later moved), so cast a wide net.

3. **Boston Pilot "Missing Persons" Database** ⭐
   - Free at **[infowanted.bc.edu](https://infowanted.bc.edu)**
   - Unique to Boston and frequently supplies the Irish county or parish of origin, arrival ship, and year — detail the passenger list itself rarely provides.

4. **Massachusetts Vital Records**
   - State-level registration began in **1841**, but 1840s coverage was incomplete.
   - Supplement with **Catholic parish registers** at the **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** — essential for Irish immigrant families.

5. **Boston City Directories**
   - Published annually from the 1820s; place a person at a specific Boston address between census years.

### Suggested Next Step

Build a research plan that sequences these sources for your specific ancestor — starting with the Boston Pilot Missing Persons database, then the passenger list collection, then naturalization records in Massachusetts and any states the family later moved to.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840–1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Port:** Port of Boston, one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s
- **County:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Massachusetts (state since 1788)
- **Population during period:** By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the surge of Famine-era immigration (1845–1852). Boston was a compact, rapidly urbanizing city; immigrants settled primarily in the North End and Fort Hill neighborhoods.
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, manufacturing, commerce. The port's relative affordability compared to New York made it the preferred landfall for many Irish and some British, German, and Canadian immigrants.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Irish (especially after 1845), with British, German, and smaller Canadian and other European communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish immigrants), Protestant Episcopal, Congregationalist, Methodist, Baptist.
- **Key historical events:** Irish Great Famine (1845–1852) drove the largest single wave of immigration through Boston in the 19th century. The period also saw the arrival of German political refugees after 1848.

## Boundary changes
- Boston was coextensive with Suffolk County for this period; no significant boundary changes affected the port or record-keeping jurisdiction between 1840 and 1860.
- Massachusetts became a state in 1788; all federal and state record systems were in place by the target period.

## Available record types

### Passenger lists (customs manifests)
- **Start date:** Federal customs passenger lists required from 1820 under the Passenger Act.
- **What exists:** Customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston, 1820–1891, are in National Archives Record Group 36. The 1840s lists record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the detailed town of origin or next-of-kin data found in post-1895 manifests.

If your ancestor arrived in Boston but later appears in Pennsylvania, trace the onward migration through city directories, naturalization records filed in Pennsylvania, and the 1850 and 1855 censuses.

Here is what the locality-guide agent returned:

---

You are researching ancestors connected to Native American tribes in what is now **Oklahoma** during the mid-1800s — a region then called **Indian Territory**, under federal oversight and tribal self-government, with no state civil registration system until after Oklahoma statehood in 1907.

**The most important records are:**

- **Tribal enrollment rolls** — especially the **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** and earlier **pre-Dawes rolls from the 1850s**
- **BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs) agency annuity payment rolls**
- **Missionary church registers**, which go back to the 1820s

**Where to find them:**

- The **Dawes Rolls** and early land records are indexed and searchable online **for free on FamilySearch**
- The underlying **BIA agency correspondence** and many **tribal court records** are physical-only at the **National Archives in Fort Worth, Texas**
- The **Oklahoma Historical Society** in Oklahoma City holds additional tribal and territorial records

---

**Critical next step:** Identify which specific tribe the family belonged to, because every major record series in Indian Territory is organized **by nation rather than by territory as a whole**. A Cherokee family's records live in a completely different set than a Chickasaw or Creek family's — searching the wrong series will yield nothing even when the records exist.
