added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties. Pittsburgh incorporated as a borough in 1794 and as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data for the specific city was not returned by the population tool during this survey; consult census volumes directly. The broader region grew rapidly — Carnegie's steel expansion from the 1870s onward drove dramatic in-migration.
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated; Carnegie Steel and associated firms employed hundreds of thousands. Glassmaking, coking, and coal transport were secondary industries. The Monongahela and Allegheny river valleys were lined with mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne) that functioned as separate municipalities.
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigrant labor force from Ireland, Germany, Poland, Slovakia, Croatia, and Italy arrived in successive waves through the late 1800s. Earlier settlers were predominantly Scots-Irish and German.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran, Greek Catholic (Ruthenian/Ukrainian), Jewish congregations in significant numbers by 1880s.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike of 1892 (Carnegie Steel vs. Amalgamated Association); Johnstown Flood 1889 (affected many Pittsburgh-area workers); rapid industrialization 1870s–1900s drove one of the largest internal migrations in US history.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries have been stable since 1800.
- **Critical:** The city of Allegheny (present-day Pittsburgh's North Side) was an independent municipality with its own records until it was annexed by Pittsburgh in 1907. Records for North Side families before 1907 may be filed under 'Allegheny City,' not 'Pittsburgh.'
- Numerous mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne, Munhall) remained separate incorporated boroughs throughout this period. Families living in these towns generated records under those municipalities, not Pittsburgh proper.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration until 1906 (state level). No reliable statewide birth, marriage, or death registration system existed for the period 1860–1905. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey; for the definitive start dates at each level, consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records) directly.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records with images — indexed + images). Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317, 524,189 indexed records). Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957, 312,045 records). Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909, 198,765 records, images not available online).
- **Where held:** Post-1906 certificates: Pennsylvania State Archives and local registrars. Pre-1906: no systematic civil system — see church records below.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths 1860–1905 have no statewide civil record. Local registrations were inconsistent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the primary substitute. Federal census mortality schedules (1860, 1870, 1880) record deaths in the year preceding the census and are a partial gap-filler.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian parishes — each ethnicity typically had its own separate parish); Presbyterian; Methodist; Lutheran; Greek Catholic; Episcopal; Jewish synagogues.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Ethnic parishes also often maintained membership lists and death registers in the heritage language.
- **Where held:** Individual parish offices; diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh for Roman Catholics); FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Church Records returned only generic content during this survey — consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records) for current repository details.
- **Language:** Irish and German Catholic registers may be partly in Latin; Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian registers may be in those vernacular languages.
- **Critical note:** Ethnic Catholic parishes each maintained their own registers — a Polish steelworker's baptism will be in the Polish parish register, not an Irish or generic Catholic one. Identifying which ethnic parish served a given community is essential before searching church records.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 — all available and indexed for Allegheny County. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire and is unavailable. All decennial censuses list occupation, which is essential for identifying steel workers.
- **1880 census special schedules:** The 1880 defective, dependent, and delinquent schedules (DDD) list individuals in institutions.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding the census — a partial substitute for missing vital records.
- **Access:** Federal census records for this period are indexed and available at FamilySearch (free), Ancestry.com, and MyHeritage.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, inventories, guardianships. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images online but 0 indexed records — browse-only. The statewide volume_search also returned a probate volume (DGS 008120441, 1,180 images, covering 1683–1994) with 0% name-indexing and not full-text searchable — browse-only images.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills, Pittsburgh (originals). FamilySearch has images.
- **Court records:** The Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas handled naturalizations (pre-1906), civil suits, and guardianships. Court minute books also record routine county business that names ordinary residents.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania is a state-land state (metes and bounds, not the rectangular federal survey). Land patents were granted by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. Property tax lists are particularly useful for the 1860–1905 gap in vital records — annual assessment lists can place a family at a specific address each year.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania General Land Office (historical) and the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (for deed transfers). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property) directly.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds for post-formation deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for earlier patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) affected the generation born 1830–1848; Spanish-American War (1898). Many Pittsburgh-area men served in Pennsylvania volunteer regiments.
- **Record types:** Union service records and pension files at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) indexes Civil War pension and service files.
- **Occupational military connection:** The Homestead Strike of 1892 resulted in military intervention; Pennsylvania National Guard muster records for that period may document local men.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (Pittsburgh's largest 19th-century cemetery), Calvary Catholic Cemetery, St. Mary's Cemetery, and numerous denominational and ethnic cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has significant Allegheny County coverage — many Pittsburgh-area cemeteries have been transcribed. BillionGraves also has some coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for major cemeteries are held by the cemetery offices and by the Heinz History Center.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Gazette (established 1786, continuous through this period), Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Press, Pittsburgh Dispatch. Ethnic newspapers existed for German, Polish, and Slovak communities by the 1880s–1890s.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, accounts of industrial accidents (which were common in steel mills), strike coverage, and immigrant community news.
- **Where held:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds extensive local newspaper microfilm. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) have some Pittsburgh papers digitized.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most European immigrants to Pittsburgh arrived through the Port of Baltimore or Philadelphia in the earlier period, and through New York (Ellis Island, from 1892) for the later wave of Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (NARA; indexed at Ancestry.com and FamilySearch); naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia. FamilySearch has a Naturalization Records volume (DGS 008120443, 351 images, 1790–1915) at 15% name-indexed — partially searchable, partially browse-only.
- **Pre-1906 naturalization:** Before 1906, naturalizations could be filed in ANY court of record — federal, state, or local. Search the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court records at NARA Philadelphia, and city court records.
- **Content note:** Post-1906 naturalization petitions (filed under the Basic Naturalization Act) collected detailed personal information including birthplace, physical description, spouse, and children's names — far more genealogically useful than pre-1906 declarations.
- **Passenger list note:** Manifests record all persons aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. When tracing immigrant families, examine the full manifest page — siblings and other family members traveling together are listed together.

### Industrial and occupational records (specialty for this locality)
- **Company employment records:** Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and successor companies generated employment rolls and personnel records. These are fragmentary — not all survived. The Heinz History Center (https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/) holds records from several steel companies and is the first repository to contact.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area:** Archives at Homestead hold records related to the Homestead Works and the 1892 strike. Contact them directly for access.
- **Union records:** The Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers maintained membership records; the United Steelworkers of America (formed 1942) archive is at the Historical Collections and Labor Archives at Penn State University Libraries.
- **City directories:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds Pittsburgh city directories from the 1810s. These annual volumes list residents by name with occupation and address — an essential tool for tracking steel workers between censuses. Not comprehensively indexed online; must be browsed.
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania published annual reports of the Bureau of Industrial Statistics (from 1872) and factory inspector reports listing mill names, locations, and workforce numbers. Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and some research libraries.
- **Access:** Industrial employment records are largely physical-only and fragmented. City directories and factory reports require in-person or mail access.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property assessment lists and personal property tax records, generated annually.
- **Substitute value:** Annual tax lists can document a worker's presence at a specific address in every year from 1860 to 1910, filling the gap between decennial censuses and compensating for the lack of pre-1906 vital records.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County and the Pennsylvania State Archives. Some have been microfilmed.

### Other record types
- **School records:** Pittsburgh public school enrollment records exist at the Pittsburgh Public Schools archives and the Heinz History Center. Parochial school records are at individual parish offices.
- **Institutional records:** Allegheny County Poor Farm records, hospital records (Western Pennsylvania Hospital, Mercy Hospital), and orphanage records exist in scattered repositories — the Heinz History Center is the starting point.
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories from the late 19th and early 20th centuries often list founding families, carry biographical sketches, and reprint early records. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds a strong local history collection.
- **DNA and genetic genealogy:** Given the multi-ethnic immigrant character of Pittsburgh's steel workforce, Y-DNA testing can help identify male-line ethnic origin and surname variants across language boundaries (e.g., Anglicized Slovak or Polish names). GEDmatch, FamilyTreeDNA, and 23andMe are the main platforms.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | PA County Marriages 1885–1950 (collection 1921317); PA Probate Records 1683–1994 — browse-only images (1999196); PA Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317); PA Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957); PA Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909); Naturalization Records 1790–1915 — partially indexed (DGS 008120443) | Free |
| Ancestry.com (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all available years) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records for Allegheny County | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records — Civil War service, pensions | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; naturalization records; federal census originals | Free/fee |
| Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) | Digitized historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search tool resolved queries to Pennsylvania statewide rather than Allegheny County specifically, returning 3 total volumes. These are statewide containers; the survey did not enumerate Allegheny County-specific digitized volumes — the true count of available digitized volumes for this locality is unknown from this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Steel company records, city directories, labor records, institutional records, photographs | In-person; contact for research services |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area, Homestead | Homestead Works records, 1892 strike records | In-person; contact archives |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1810s, local history collection, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digital access |
| Allegheny County Courthouse / Register of Wills | Probate records, deed records, naturalization records (pre-1906) | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State-level vital records post-1906, factory inspector reports, state land records, military records | In-person / online request |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA Region 3) | Federal court naturalization records, passenger lists, federal census originals | In-person / duplication request |
| Penn State University Libraries — Historical Collections and Labor Archives | United Steelworkers of America records | In-person / contact |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact for access |

## Records NOT online

- Company employment records (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and others) — held at the Heinz History Center; fragmentary survival; physical access only.
- Pittsburgh city directories (pre-digital era) — held at Carnegie Library; must be browsed in person or on microfilm.
- Pre-1906 birth and death records — no systematic civil system; church registers are the substitute, held at parishes and diocesan archives.
- Allegheny County property tax assessment lists — held at county and state archives; not comprehensively digitized.
- Ethnic parish registers (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) — many held at individual parishes or diocesan archives; not systematically online.
- State factory inspector and Bureau of Industrial Statistics reports — at Pennsylvania State Archives; not online.
- Allegheny City (pre-1907 North Side) municipal records — held at Allegheny County or Pittsburgh City archives; distinguish carefully from Pittsburgh city records.

## Known record losses

No specific record destruction events for Pittsburgh or Allegheny County were returned by the tools during this survey. The 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire nationally — this gap affects Pittsburgh research as it does all US localities. For specific information about survival of Allegheny County courthouse or church records, contact the Heinz History Center and the Pennsylvania State Archives directly.

## Research tips

- **Identify the ethnic community first.** In Pittsburgh's steel workforce, ethnic identity largely determined which parish a family attended and which neighborhood they lived in. Identifying ethnicity from the census (birthplace, parents' birthplaces, language spoken) is the gateway to the correct church register. [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial and Occupational Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records]
- **Use city directories as annual census substitutes.** Because federal censuses run only every ten years and pre-1906 vital records are sparse, Pittsburgh city directories (Carnegie Library, from the 1810s) can place a family at a specific address with occupation in virtually every year of the period. This is the single most powerful tool for tracking a mobile working-class family between censuses. [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records]
- **Search Allegheny City separately from Pittsburgh.** The city of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was independent until 1907. If a family is missing from Pittsburgh records before 1907, search under 'Allegheny City.'
- **Search mill towns separately.** Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne, Munhall, and other mill towns were separate municipalities with their own record systems. A steel worker at the Homestead Works lived in Homestead, not Pittsburgh — search Homestead's records.
- **Check naturalization records at multiple courts.** Before 1906, a man could declare his intention and be naturalized in any court — county, state, or federal. Search the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court (NARA Philadelphia), and any city court records. [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records]
- **Post-1906 naturalizations are more informative.** The Basic Naturalization Act of 1906 standardized the process and required extensive personal information — birthplace, physical description, spouse's name, children's names and ages. A naturalization after 1906 is often the most information-dense document in a steel worker immigrant's file.
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records (FamilySearch collection 1999196)** has over 3.2 million images but zero indexed records — it must be browsed image by image with no name search. Use the finding aids at the Allegheny County Register of Wills to identify the volume and page before browsing.
- **Consider the 1892 Homestead Strike as a locating event.** Workers involved in the strike appear in newspaper accounts, court records (prosecutions for conspiracy), and National Guard muster records — a documented moment that can place a specific man in the Homestead Works.
- **Naming conventions:** German and some Irish families followed generational naming patterns (eldest son named for paternal grandfather, etc.). Polish, Slovak, and Croatian names were frequently anglicized on arrival — a 'Steve Horvath' may be recorded as 'Istvan Horvath' in church registers. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Naming Customs returned only generic content; consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naming_Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naming_Customs) directly for detailed guidance.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Allegheny County borders Butler, Armstrong, Westmoreland, Washington, and Beaver Counties. Steel and glass workers often crossed county lines for work or lived just outside the Pittsburgh city limits. If a family cannot be found in Allegheny County records, search the bordering counties — particularly Westmoreland (Monessen, Donora) and Washington (Charleroi) which also had steel and glass industries.

**Philadelphia During the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Records & Repositories**
*(Locality guide saved as **loc_001** in research.json)*

---

### Key Finding: No Civil Death Records Exist
Pennsylvania did not require civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906**. This means there are no government death certificates for epidemic victims. **Church burial registers are the only systematic death record for this period**, surviving in scattered church archives, at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), and on FamilySearch microfilm.

| Record Type | Repository | Notes |

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1785–1810, Focus on 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682; the city of Philadelphia incorporated 1701
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county were effectively coextensive by the late 18th century)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making Philadelphia the largest city in the United States and its capital at the time
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic seaport; commerce, shipping, trade, crafts, and early manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English and Welsh Quakers in founding generations; substantial German, Scots-Irish, and Irish immigrant communities by the late 18th century; a free Black population documented by the African Methodist Episcopal Church records
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1794)
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783); Philadelphia served as national capital 1790–1800; yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population; recurring yellow fever outbreaks 1794–1798

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was formed in 1682 and its boundaries were stable throughout the target period. No boundary changes affected the county during 1785–1810.
- The city of Philadelphia proper occupied a small portion of the county in 1793; the surrounding districts (Southwark, Northern Liberties, Kensington, Germantown) were separate municipalities within the county. Records for residents of those districts may be filed under the district name, not "Philadelphia city."
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 merged the city and all surrounding districts into a single entity — but that is after this period. For 1793 research, always check whether a family lived in the city proper or in one of the surrounding districts.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. No civil vital records were created for the 1793 epidemic period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey — confirm the precise registration history directly at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers are the only systematic vital records for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire period 1785–1810 predates civil registration. Vital events are documented solely through church records, Quaker meeting minutes, newspaper notices, and private family papers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers (see Church records below); newspaper death notices; the Mathew Carey published account listing epidemic dead; the Bush Hill hospital records.

### Church records — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR 1793
- **Denominations present:** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal); Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church, Swedish Lutheran); St. Peter's Church (Episcopal); First Presbyterian; Second Presbyterian; St. Mary's (Catholic); St. Joseph's (Catholic); Methodist; Baptist; German Lutheran; German Reformed; African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1794, Richard Allen's congregation)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Burial registers for August–November 1793 are the single most important documentary source for epidemic deaths.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), the Presbyterian Historical Society, the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives, the Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives, and FamilySearch microfilm. Many early Philadelphia church registers have been transcribed and published; the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania holds indexes. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Language:** English for most Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers; German for Lutheran and German Reformed registers. Researchers must be able to read the original language.
- **Epidemic note:** Burial registers from Christ Church, Gloria Dei, and other active congregations show a sharp and documented spike in entries during August–November 1793. Because some clergy also fled, certain periods may have abbreviated entries or gaps in recording.

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793 research)
- **Mathew Carey's account:** Published in 1793 as *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia*, this widely circulated pamphlet lists names of the dead and is a unique finding aid. Multiple editions exist. Available in digitized form through archive.org and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Committee of Citizens minutes:** The Committee appointed by citizens of Philadelphia to manage relief during the epidemic kept minutes and reports that name individuals. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Documents from the improvised hospital established at Bush Hill, where many epidemic victims died. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records:** The mayor's correspondence and official records from 1793 document the city's administrative response and may name families.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (taken before the epidemic — the closest prior enumeration) and 1800 (taken after). Both are name-searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch. For families affected by the epidemic, cross-check between the 1790 and 1800 censuses; a household that shrinks or disappears may reflect epidemic losses or flight from the city.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia city directories were published in the 1790s and early 1800s and can place a person at a specific address in years between censuses. The 1793 directory, taken just before the epidemic, is particularly useful.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and image-available on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). City directories are available in digitized form through the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Internet Archive.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate), estate inventories, guardianship files. A sharp increase in probate filings is expected in late 1793 and 1794, directly reflecting epidemic deaths.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County Register of Wills, which has records back to the colonial period. FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) holds 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 records indexed). Researchers must browse image by image; there is no name index within this FamilySearch collection.
- **Substitute / index:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold some compiled indexes to early Philadelphia probate. The Register of Wills in Philadelphia may also hold a separate in-house index.
- **Research tip:** For 1793, search for wills proved and administrations granted in late 1793 and through 1794 — the probate surge from epidemic deaths is well documented and the records are rich with family relationship data.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was not distributed through the federal rectangular survey system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania granted land through the Pennsylvania Land Office; original grants and patents are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (a distinctive Philadelphia tenure form), tax assessment lists.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County deed books at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Recorder of Deeds. Tax assessment lists (which can substitute for census years and place a family on a specific property) are held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the HSP.
- **Date range:** Deed records available from the late 17th century.
- **Online status:** Not comprehensively indexed for 1793. Physical or microfilm access required for most deed searches.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The period 1785–1810 includes the Quasi-War (1798–1800) and the lead-up to the War of 1812. The Revolutionary War (ended 1783) is just before this period but pension and bounty land files created after 1793 are relevant.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files (filed from 1818 onward under various acts); bounty land warrants; Pennsylvania militia records; muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files and federal service records); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records). Fold3 (subscription) has digitized NARA military collections. Revolutionary War pension files are indexed and browsable on Fold3 and Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground; Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard; St. Peter's churchyard; numerous other church burial grounds; Potter's Field (for the indigent, including many epidemic victims).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has volunteer-contributed transcriptions for many Philadelphia church cemeteries, including some 1793 epidemic burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held with the individual church archives. Christ Church burial records have been transcribed and published. The Potter's Field records for 1793 are a critical source for the urban poor who died in the epidemic.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *General Advertiser*, *Pennsylvania Packet*, *Federal Gazette*, and others published in Philadelphia in 1793. These carried death notices, lists of the sick, and accounts of families fleeing the city during August–November 1793.
- **Where held:** Digitized collections through Newspapers.com (subscription) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (free). Physical runs at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and death notices from August–November 1793 directly document epidemic deaths. Legal notices (estate administration, property sales) in the months following the epidemic name heirs and surviving family members.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was itself a major port of entry. Passenger arrival records for the 1780s–1800s are held at NARA and are indexed on Ancestry (subscription).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed in Philadelphia courts, pre-1906).
- **Where held:** NARA; Philadelphia City Archives for court naturalizations.
- **Epidemic context:** Thousands of Philadelphia residents fled the city during the epidemic, many to surrounding counties. This is an emigration event in reverse — some may appear in Chester, Montgomery, Bucks, or Delaware county records during August–November 1793.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia city and county tax assessment lists (property tax, personal property).
- **Date range:** Available from the late 18th century.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Some years have been transcribed.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for census records in non-census years (e.g., 1791–1799) and place a family at a specific address or document property they held.

### Other record types
- **Published local and family histories:** The 19th- and early-20th-century tradition of published county and city histories produced substantial biographical and genealogical material about Philadelphia families. The Library Company of Philadelphia and the HSP hold extensive collections. WorldCat can locate copies.
- **Quaker meeting minutes:** 1 digitized volume is held by FamilySearch (image group 001188322, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, 145 images). This volume is browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be read image by image. The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives holds additional manuscript records.
- **African American records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) and the African Methodist Episcopal Church (founded 1794 by Richard Allen) kept membership and burial records. The AME church specifically documented Black epidemic victims and relief workers in 1793. Records are held at the AME church archives and the HSP.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records, indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790 and 1800 (indexed + images); passenger lists; Revolutionary War pension files; some Philadelphia church records | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records — Revolutionary War pensions, service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia church burial grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) | Historical Philadelphia newspapers 1790s | Subscription |
| Internet Archive (https://archive.org) | Mathew Carey's 1793 account; digitized Philadelphia city directories | Free |
| Library of Congress Chronicling America | Digitized Philadelphia newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period; this is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections, of which 3 overlap the pre-1906 period relevant to this research. The wiki_place_page calls for all four sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic fallback page rather than Philadelphia- or Pennsylvania-specific content, representing a coverage gap in this tool survey — researchers should consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), Philadelphia | Committee of Citizens minutes (1793); church register transcriptions; city directories; tax lists; family papers; published histories | In-person; some digitized through HSP Digital Library |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Bush Hill hospital records; deed records; tax assessments; city administrative records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Pennsylvania land patents; colonial and state government records | In-person; some online via PA Digital |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; some indexes published |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Published local histories; city directories; pamphlets including Carey's 1793 account | In-person |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives | Quaker meeting records, minutes, membership lists | In-person or written inquiry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church registers and minutes | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic sacramental registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives | Episcopal/Anglican church registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal court records; naturalization petitions; federal census originals | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Church burial registers for most individual Philadelphia congregations (except those microfilmed by FamilySearch or transcribed by the GSP)
- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports (1793)
- Bush Hill hospital records (1793)
- Mayor's correspondence and administrative records (1793)
- Philadelphia County deed books for the 1790s (not comprehensively digitized or indexed)
- Philadelphia city tax assessment lists for most years in the 1790s
- Philadelphia Yearly Meeting manuscript records beyond the 1 digitized FamilySearch volume
- Sexton and burial ground records for most individual churches

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey named specific record losses for Philadelphia church registers or city records from the 1793 period. The Philadelphia City Archives and HSP are the repositories to contact to confirm whether specific record sets survived. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia returned only generic content in this survey, so no specific loss claims can be grounded in tool output. Researchers should not assume records are lost simply because they are not online.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's 1793 account.** This published list of the dead is a unique finding aid available free through the Internet Archive. It directly names individuals who died in the epidemic and is the fastest entry point for confirming whether an ancestor was among the documented dead. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))
- **Cross the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** A household present in 1790 but absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths or the flight of families who never returned. Note that the 1790 census records only the head of household by name.
- **Search the surrounding counties for 1793.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during August–November 1793. Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, and Chester counties may hold church, tax, or court records documenting these families during their temporary relocation. Search those county records for the period even if the family is known as Philadelphia residents.
- **Church burial registers are the primary death record.** Pennsylvania did not require civil registration until 1906. For 1793, every death is documented (if at all) in a church burial register, not a government certificate. Identify the family's denomination first, then locate that congregation's register. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Check probate filings for late 1793 and 1794.** Estate administrations filed immediately after the epidemic are rich with family relationship data — naming surviving spouses, children, and creditors. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) holds 3.2 million images but is 0% name-indexed: it must be browsed. Use any in-house index at the Philadelphia Register of Wills or GSP compiled indexes to locate specific entries.
- **The African American community kept its own records.** The Free African Society (1787) and AME Church (1794) documented Black Philadelphians who both died in the epidemic and provided substantial relief care. These records at the AME archives and HSP are essential for African American family research in this period.
- **Philadelphia districts matter.** In 1793, Southwark, Northern Liberties, and Germantown were separate municipalities. Records for a family in those areas may be filed under the district name, not under Philadelphia city. Confirm the specific address before routing a search.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled indexes** are a critical finding aid for accessing Philadelphia church records before searching individual parish registers. Consult their holdings at the HSP before attempting to browse unindexed volumes.
- **Philadelphia city directories from the 1790s** place individuals at specific street addresses in non-census years and can document whether a person remained in the city after the epidemic or relocated. Digitized copies are available through Internet Archive.

- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei / Old Swedes'), African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1794)
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783); Philadelphia served as national capital 1790–1800; yellow fever epidemic August–November 1793, killing approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population; recurring yellow fever outbreaks 1794–1798

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was formed in 1682 and its boundaries were stable throughout the target period. No boundary changes affected the county during 1785–1810.
- The city of Philadelphia proper occupied a small portion of the county in 1793; the surrounding districts (Southwark, Northern Liberties, Kensington, Germantown) were separate municipalities within the county. Records for residents of those districts may be filed under the district name, not "Philadelphia city."
- The Consolidation Act of 1854 merged the city and all surrounding districts into a single entity — but that is after this period. For 1793 research, always check whether a family lived in the city proper or in one of the surrounding districts.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until 1906. No civil vital records were created for the 1793 epidemic period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only generic content in this survey — confirm the precise registration history directly at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates. Church registers are the only systematic vital records for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire period 1785–1810 predates civil registration. Vital events are documented solely through church records, Quaker meeting minutes, newspaper notices, and private family papers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers (see Church records below); newspaper death notices; the Mathew Carey published account listing epidemic dead; the Bush Hill hospital records.

### Church records — PRIMARY SOURCE FOR 1793
- **Denominations present:** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal); Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church, Swedish Lutheran); St. Peter's Church (Episcopal); First Presbyterian; Second Presbyterian; St. Mary's (Catholic); St. Joseph's (Catholic); Methodist; Baptist; German Lutheran; German Reformed; African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1794, Richard Allen's congregation)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Burial registers for August–November 1793 are the single most important documentary source for epidemic deaths.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), the Presbyterian Historical Society, the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives, the Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives, and FamilySearch microfilm. Many early Philadelphia church registers have been transcribed and published; the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania holds indexes. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Language:** English for most Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist records; Latin for Catholic sacramental registers; German for Lutheran and German Reformed registers. Researchers must be able to read the original language.
- **Epidemic note:** Burial registers from Christ Church, Gloria Dei, and other active congregations show a sharp and documented spike in entries during August–November 1793. Because some clergy also fled, certain periods may have abbreviated entries or gaps in recording.

### Epidemic-specific sources (unique to 1793 research)
- **Mathew Carey's account:** Published in 1793 as *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia*, this widely circulated pamphlet lists names of the dead and is a unique finding aid. Multiple editions exist. Available in digitized form through archive.org and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Committee of Citizens minutes:** The Committee appointed by citizens of Philadelphia to manage relief during the epidemic kept minutes and reports that name individuals. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Bush Hill hospital records:** Documents from the improvised hospital established at Bush Hill, where many epidemic victims died. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records:** The mayor's correspondence and official records from 1793 document the city's administrative response and may name families.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 (taken before the epidemic — the closest prior enumeration) and 1800 (taken after). Both are name-searchable on Ancestry and FamilySearch. For families affected by the epidemic, cross-check between the 1790 and 1800 censuses; a household that shrinks or disappears may reflect epidemic losses or flight from the city.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Philadelphia city directories were published in the 1790s and early 1800s and can place a person at a specific address in years between censuses. The 1793 directory, taken just before the epidemic, is particularly useful.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and image-available on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). City directories are available in digitized form through the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Internet Archive.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate), estate inventories, guardianship files. A sharp increase in probate filings is expected in late 1793 and 1794, directly reflecting epidemic deaths.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County Register of Wills, which has records back to the colonial period. FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) holds 3,200,560 images — browse-only (0 records indexed). Researchers must browse image by image; there is no name index within this FamilySearch collection.
- **Substitute / index:** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania hold some compiled indexes to early Philadelphia probate. The Register of Wills in Philadelphia may also hold a separate in-house index.
- **Research tip:** For 1793, search for wills proved and administrations granted in late 1793 and through 1794 — the probate surge from epidemic deaths is well documented and the records are rich with family relationship data.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was not distributed through the federal rectangular survey system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania granted land through the Pennsylvania Land Office; original grants and patents are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (a distinctive Philadelphia tenure form), tax assessment lists.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County deed books at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Recorder of Deeds. Tax assessment lists (which can substitute for census years and place a family on a specific property) are held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the HSP.
- **Date range:** Deed records available from the late 17th century.
- **Online status:** Not comprehensively indexed for 1793. Physical or microfilm access required for most deed searches.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The period 1785–1810 includes the Quasi-War (1798–1800) and the lead-up to the War of 1812. The Revolutionary War (ended 1783) is just before this period but pension and bounty land files created after 1793 are relevant.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files (filed from 1818 onward under various acts); bounty land warrants; Pennsylvania militia records; muster rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (pension files and federal service records); Pennsylvania State Archives (militia records). Fold3 (subscription) has digitized NARA military collections. Revolutionary War pension files are indexed and browsable on Fold3 and Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Christ Church Burial Ground; Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') churchyard; St. Peter's churchyard; numerous other church burial grounds; Potter's Field (for the indigent, including many epidemic victims).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has volunteer-contributed transcriptions for many Philadelphia church cemeteries, including some 1793 epidemic burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held with the individual church archives. Christ Church burial records have been transcribed and published. The Potter's Field records for 1793 are a critical source for the urban poor who died in the epidemic.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *General Advertiser*, *Pennsylvania Packet*, *Federal Gazette*, and others published in Philadelphia in 1793. These carried death notices, lists of the sick, and accounts of families fleeing the city during August–November 1793.
- **Where held:** Digitized collections through Newspapers.com (subscription) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (free). Physical runs at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Library Company of Philadelphia.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and death notices from August–November 1793 directly document epidemic deaths. Legal notices (estate administration, property sales) in the months following the epidemic name heirs and surviving family members.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was itself a major port of entry. Passenger arrival records for the 1780s–1800s are held at NARA and are indexed on Ancestry (subscription).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists; declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed in Philadelphia courts, pre-1906).
- **Where held:** NARA; Philadelphia City Archives for court naturalizations.
- **Epidemic context:** Thousands of Philadelphia residents fled the city during the epidemic, many to surrounding counties. This is an emigration event in reverse — some may appear in Chester, Montgomery, Bucks, or Delaware county records during August–November 1793.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Philadelphia city and county tax assessment lists (property tax, personal property).
- **Date range:** Available from the late 18th century.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Some years have been transcribed.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for census records in non-census years (e.g., 1791–1799) and place a family at a specific address or document property they held.

### Other record types
- **Published local and family histories:** The 19th- and early-20th-century tradition of published county and city histories produced substantial biographical and genealogical material about Philadelphia families. The Library Company of Philadelphia and the HSP hold extensive collections. WorldCat can locate copies.
- **Quaker meeting minutes:** 1 digitized volume is held by FamilySearch (image group 001188322, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, 145 images). This volume is browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be read image by image. The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives holds additional manuscript records.
- **African American records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) and the African Methodist Episcopal Church (founded 1794 by Richard Allen) kept membership and burial records. The AME church specifically documented Black epidemic victims and relief workers in 1793. Records are held at the AME church archives and the HSP.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records, indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records, indexed); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (145 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1790 and 1800 (indexed + images); passenger lists; Revolutionary War pension files; some Philadelphia church records | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military records — Revolutionary War pensions, service records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia church burial grounds | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) | Historical Philadelphia newspapers 1790s | Subscription |
| Internet Archive (https://archive.org) | Mathew Carey's 1793 account; digitized Philadelphia city directories | Free |
| Library of Congress Chronicling America | Digitized Philadelphia newspapers | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for this place and period; this is the complete result set (totalResults: 1). Collections_search returned 6 Pennsylvania-level collections, of which 3 overlap the pre-1906 period relevant to this research. The wiki_place_page calls for all four sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic fallback page rather than Philadelphia- or Pennsylvania-specific content, representing a coverage gap in this tool survey — researchers should consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP), Philadelphia | Committee of Citizens minutes (1793); church register transcriptions; city directories; tax lists; family papers; published histories | In-person; some digitized through HSP Digital Library |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Bush Hill hospital records; deed records; tax assessments; city administrative records | In-person or written inquiry |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | Pennsylvania land patents; colonial and state government records | In-person; some online via PA Digital |
| Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records | In-person; some indexes published |
| Library Company of Philadelphia | Published local histories; city directories; pamphlets including Carey's 1793 account | In-person |
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives | Quaker meeting records, minutes, membership lists | In-person or written inquiry |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia | Presbyterian church registers and minutes | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic sacramental registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania Archives | Episcopal/Anglican church registers | In-person or written inquiry |
| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Federal court records; naturalization petitions; federal census originals | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Church burial registers for most individual Philadelphia congregations (except those microfilmed by FamilySearch or transcribed by the GSP)
- Committee of Citizens minutes and reports (1793)
- Bush Hill hospital records (1793)
- Mayor's correspondence and administrative records (1793)
- Philadelphia County deed books for the 1790s (not comprehensively digitized or indexed)
- Philadelphia city tax assessment lists for most years in the 1790s
- Philadelphia Yearly Meeting manuscript records beyond the 1 digitized FamilySearch volume
- Sexton and burial ground records for most individual churches

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey named specific record losses for Philadelphia church registers or city records from the 1793 period. The Philadelphia City Archives and HSP are the repositories to contact to confirm whether specific record sets survived. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Philadelphia returned only generic content in this survey, so no specific loss claims can be grounded in tool output. Researchers should not assume records are lost simply because they are not online.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's 1793 account.** This published list of the dead is a unique finding aid available free through the Internet Archive. It directly names individuals who died in the epidemic and is the fastest entry point for confirming whether an ancestor was among the documented dead. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))
- **Cross the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** A household present in 1790 but absent or reduced in 1800 may reflect epidemic deaths or the flight of families who never returned. Note that the 1790 census records only the head of household by name.
- **Search the surrounding counties for 1793.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during August–November 1793. Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, and Chester counties may hold church, tax, or court records documenting these families during their temporary relocation. Search those county records for the period even if the family is known as Philadelphia residents.
- **Church burial registers are the primary death record.** Pennsylvania did not require civil registration until 1906. For 1793, every death is documented (if at all) in a church burial register, not a government certificate. Identify the family's denomination first, then locate that congregation's register. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Check probate filings for late 1793 and 1794.** Estate administrations filed immediately after the epidemic are rich with family relationship data — naming surviving spouses, children, and creditors. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1999196) holds 3.2 million images but is 0% name-indexed: it must be browsed. Use any in-house index at the Philadelphia Register of Wills or GSP compiled indexes to locate specific entries.
- **The African American community kept its own records.** The Free African Society (1787) and AME Church (1794) documented Black Philadelphians who both died in the epidemic and provided substantial relief care. These records at the AME archives and HSP are essential for African American family research in this period.
- **Philadelphia districts matter.** In 1793, Southwark, Northern Liberties, and Germantown were separate municipalities. Records for a family in those areas may be filed under the district name, not under Philadelphia city. Confirm the specific address before routing a search.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's compiled indexes** are a critical finding aid for accessing Philadelphia church records before searching individual parish registers. Consult their holdings at the HSP before attempting to browse unindexed volumes.
- **Philadelphia city directories from the 1790s** place individuals at specific street addresses in non-census years and can document whether a person remained in the city after the epidemic or relocated. Digitized copies are available through Internet Archive.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

Researching families in Chicago around the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 requires working around one of the most significant record losses in American genealogical history. The fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, taking with it deeds, civil birth and death registers, court records, tax rolls, and pre-fire probate files.

What survives falls into two distinct layers:

**Pre-Fire Layer**
- **1870 Federal Census** — The most important surviving pre-fire source. Originals were held in Washington and escaped destruction. Indexed on FamilySearch.
- **Church registers** — Parishes that kept registers at the parish house (rather than the courthouse) may have survived. The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** is the place to determine which Catholic parish registers exist.
- **FamilySearch church records** — Cook County church records going back to 1833 are indexed on FamilySearch (~620,000+ records).

**Post-Fire Layer (records resume late 1871)**
- **Cook County civil births** — ~1.45 million records on FamilySearch, beginning 1871.
- **Cook County deaths** — ~980,000 records on FamilySearch, beginning 1871.
- **Cook County marriages** — ~620,000 records on FamilySearch, beginning 1871.
- **Reconstructed deeds (1872 Burnt Records Act)** — Property owners were required to re-record deeds; these sometimes include a history of prior ownership.
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** — Held at the **Chicago History Museum**; a direct substitute for destroyed property records.

**Displaced-Family Records**
- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** — Held at the **Chicago History Museum**. Named thousands of displaced fire victims by name — a critical unique source for families uprooted by the disaster.

**Unaffected Federal Records**
- **Bureau of Land Management federal land patents** — Held federally, not in the courthouse, so unaffected by the fire.

**Next Steps**
