# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1850–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County formed 1831; Chicago incorporated as a city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (statehood 1818)
- **Population during period:** Chicago grew from approximately 29,000 (1850) to 300,000 (1870) to over 500,000 (1880), making it one of the fastest-growing cities in the United States
- **Economy:** Lake port, railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber, grain trading, manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Scandinavian (especially Swedish and Norwegian), and smaller Polish and Bohemian immigrant communities by 1870
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant among Irish and German immigrants), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — killed approximately 300 people, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, left over 100,000 homeless, and eliminated the Cook County Courthouse and the bulk of the city's civil records

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries were stable during this period
- Chicago city limits expanded through annexations of surrounding townships throughout the 1850s–1880s; an ancestor living just outside the city may fall under a different township's records
- No parent-jurisdiction record split: Cook County was already well established before the target period begins

## The Record Loss Problem — Critical Context

The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871. According to Wikipedia's article on the fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), the courthouse housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. This creates a hard break in the documentary record:

- **Pre-1871:** Most Cook County civil records are gone. Researchers must rely entirely on substitute sources (see below).
- **Post-1871:** Civil registration resumed quickly. Cook County vital records, court records, and land records from late 1871 onward survive.

According to the FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire), genealogists must use substitute sources: reconstructed deeds filed under the Burnt Record Act (1872), church registers from parishes that survived or were re-established, insurance company records (especially the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum), and the federal census schedules for 1850, 1860, and 1870 — the 1870 schedules survived because the originals were held in Washington.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Cook County began recording vital events at the county level; however, the pre-fire records were destroyed. Surviving county-level vital registration begins effectively in late 1871. Illinois statewide registration did not begin until 1916.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds three indexed collections covering the post-fire period: Cook County Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (approximately 1,450,000 records, collection ID 2024189); Cook County Death Records 1871–1947 (approximately 980,000 records, collection ID 1913456); Cook County Marriage Records 1871–1920 (approximately 620,000 records, collection ID 1756321). All three are on FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's Office (originals); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed post-1871 series)
- **Gaps:** All pre-fire (pre-October 1871) civil vital records were destroyed. Events in 1871 before the fire are lost.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); 1870 federal census; city directories; newspaper notices

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations were all present by 1870
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a collection of Cook County Chicago Church Records 1833–1925 (approximately 285,000 records, collection ID 1803978). Some parish registers were kept at the parish itself and survived the fire; others were destroyed. FamilySearch has microfilmed many post-fire Cook County church records.
- **Language:** Catholic records may be in Latin; German Lutheran records in German
- **Critical note:** Church registers are the primary substitute for pre-fire civil vital registration. Not all parishes survived or kept separate copies; contact the Archdiocese archives to determine which registers survive for your specific parish

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, and 1870 federal censuses for Chicago all survive (the 1870 originals were in Washington and escaped the fire). The 1880 federal census also survives. All are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding each census; these are particularly useful for identifying fire victims and their families.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in 1855 and 1865; check the Illinois State Archives for these.
- **Access:** Federal census records for this period are indexed and images are online at FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions, naturalizations
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate records were destroyed. Post-fire records from late 1871 onward survive at Cook County.
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds many Cook County records post-1871. The Cook County Circuit Court Archives holds court records.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record. Cook County naturalizations before the fire were largely destroyed; check federal district court records at NARA's Great Lakes Region (Chicago) for possible duplicates.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal land state — land was originally distributed through the federal General Land Office
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original federal land grants and patents are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov); these records were held federally and were NOT destroyed in the fire
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **The Burnt Record Act:** The 1872 Illinois Burnt Record Act required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire. These reconstructed deeds are filed at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds. Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records at the Chicago History Museum are another key substitute source for pre-fire property ownership.
- **Date range:** Federal land patents from the 1830s onward at BLM GLO; reconstructed deeds from 1872 onward at the Recorder of Deeds
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (originals); Chicago History Museum (insurance/title records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Chicago men served in Illinois volunteer regiments
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations, unit rosters. The Civil War Draft (1863 enrollment) records are at NARA and were not destroyed in the fire
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pension files); Fold3 (digitized military records, subscription); Illinois State Archives (state-level service records)
- **Note:** Civil War pension files are particularly rich: they contain affidavits naming family members, dates and places of birth and marriage, and statements about the family's history — excellent substitutes for destroyed vital records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery, Rosehill Cemetery, and St. Boniface (Catholic) were established in this period; some south-side Catholic cemeteries also predate the fire
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) and BillionGraves have substantial Chicago coverage
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; the Chicago History Museum holds some burial records
- **Note:** Cemetery records are valuable for pre-fire events because gravestones and sexton records were not destroyed in the courthouse fire

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) survived the fire; several German-language papers served the immigrant community
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com, subscription) for digitized historical newspapers; the Newberry Library holds newspaper microfilm
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices, fire relief lists, and displaced-persons notices published in the days and weeks after the fire are particularly useful for tracing affected families

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; most immigrants arrived via the port of New York (Ellis Island era begins 1892; Castle Garden 1820–1892), Baltimore, or New Orleans and traveled inland by rail or canal
- **Record types:** Passenger lists at NARA (and Ancestry/FamilySearch); declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in Cook County courts (pre-fire largely destroyed; post-1906 at NARA); alien registrations
- **Where held:** NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) for post-1906 naturalizations; pre-1906 filings scattered across federal, state, and local courts — check all
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including infants and children; examine the full manifest for every family member. Post-fire immigrant families who were displaced may have re-immigrated or moved to other Midwest cities — check destination records in Wisconsin, Iowa, and Indiana as well

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax records
- **Pre-fire status:** Cook County tax rolls were destroyed in the fire
- **Post-fire:** Tax records resume after 1871 at the county level
- **Substitute value:** The reconstructed deeds under the Burnt Record Act partially substitute for lost tax records as evidence of property ownership

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library. They place a person at a specific address and give an occupation between census years — critical for the period when census records and other documents are missing
- **Relief records:** After the fire, the Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed aid to displaced families and kept records of recipients; these records are at the Chicago History Museum and name thousands of affected families
- **Insurance records:** Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum document pre-fire property ownership and are a direct substitute for destroyed deed records
- **Town and county histories:** Nineteenth-century published local histories (held at the Newberry Library and the Chicago History Museum) often transcribed early records and carried biographical sketches of prominent families

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Cook County Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000 records); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000 records); digitized volumes of reconstructed court and property records | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census records 1850–1880; Illinois collections | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) | Chicago Tribune and other historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military service records, pension files, Civil War records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents — NOT destroyed in the fire | Free |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records for Chicago-area cemeteries | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Military records, post-1906 naturalizations | Free finding aids; some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Chicago/Cook County in the 1850–1885 window. One volume (image group 009982110, 38 images, 1865–1871 pre-fire reconstructed county court records) is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). One volume (image group 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880 post-fire property re-recordings) is 41% name-indexed. These 2 volumes represent the complete returned result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Insurance/title records; Chicago Relief and Aid Society records; photographs; personal papers | In-person; some digitized |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s onward); maps; newspapers; local histories; manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County court and government records post-1871 | In-person; finding aids online |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward (originals) | In-person or written request |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds (1872 onward) | In-person |
| NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Post-1906 naturalizations; federal court records | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives (Springfield) | State-level records; 1855 and 1865 state censuses | In-person; some online |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-fire (pre-October 1871) Cook County civil vital records — destroyed, no online equivalent
- Pre-fire Cook County probate and court records — destroyed, no online equivalent
- Pre-fire Cook County deed records — destroyed; reconstructed Burnt Record Act deeds (1872+) are at the Recorder of Deeds, not fully digitized
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (fire victims/relief recipients) — at the Chicago History Museum, physical access
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records — at the Chicago History Museum, physical access
- Many church parish registers (especially for denominations whose parishes did not survive the fire) — contact denominational archives
- Illinois state census 1855 and 1865 — not fully indexed online; Illinois State Archives
- Cook County sexton and burial records for many cemeteries — contact individual cemeteries

## Known record losses

The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse. According to Wikipedia's article on the fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), this destroyed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms that genealogists must use substitute sources for the pre-fire period.

Not all church registers were lost: parishes that kept their registers at the parish house (rather than the courthouse) may have survived. Whether any particular parish's registers survived depends on the parish's location relative to the fire's path and its record-keeping practices — contact the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives to determine which Catholic parish registers exist and which do not.

The federal census records (1850, 1860, 1870) survived because the originals were held in Washington. BLM General Land Office federal patent records also survived. Post-fire records from late 1871 onward are substantially intact.

## Research tips

- **Start with the 1870 federal census.** It is the last surviving pre-fire census for Chicago and captures families before the disaster. Cross-reference with city directories from the Newberry Library to establish address and occupation. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County genealogy page — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **Search the Chicago Relief and Aid Society records.** After the fire, this organization distributed aid to displaced families and maintained records at the Chicago History Museum naming thousands of recipients. These records are among the few direct sources naming families specifically affected by the fire. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Use the Burnt Record Act deeds as a bridge.** Property owners who re-registered under the 1872 Act often recited the history of their property ownership in their re-recorded deed, preserving pre-fire chain-of-title information.
- **Check church registers before and after the fire separately.** A parish that survived may have pre-fire baptism and marriage registers intact; one destroyed in the fire may have reconstructed its register from memory in the months after. Contact the Archdiocese archives for the status of each parish.
- **Civil War pension files can substitute for destroyed vital records.** If a family member served in the Civil War, his pension file will contain sworn affidavits about birth date and place, marriage date and place, and children — all of which are invaluable substitutes for the records destroyed in 1871.
- **Search German-language newspapers** for immigrant families. Chicago had a substantial German-language press before and after the fire; obituaries and marriage notices appeared there rather than in the Tribune.
- **Fire-era newspaper notices.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of displaced persons and relief recipients in October–November 1871; these can place a family at a specific relief station or temporary address immediately after the fire.
- **Illinois land patents are at the BLM GLO** (https://glorecords.blm.gov) and were not affected by the courthouse fire — original federal land grants are fully intact.

| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Cook County Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000 records); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000 records); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000 records); digitized volumes of reconstructed court and property records | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | Federal census records 1850–1880; Illinois collections | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com) | Chicago Tribune and other historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military service records, pension files, Civil War records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents — NOT destroyed in the fire | Free |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery records for Chicago-area cemeteries | Free |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov) | Military records, post-1906 naturalizations | Free finding aids; some online |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Chicago/Cook County in the 1850–1885 window. One volume (image group 009982110, 38 images, 1865–1871 pre-fire reconstructed county court records) is browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). One volume (image group 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880 post-fire property re-recordings) is 41% name-indexed. These 2 volumes represent the complete returned result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Chicago History Museum | Insurance/title records; Chicago Relief and Aid Society records; photographs; personal papers | In-person; some digitized |
| Newberry Library | City directories (1840s onward); maps; newspapers; local histories; manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County court and government records post-1871 | In-person; finding aids online |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact for access |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward (originals) | In-person or written request |
| Cook County Recorder of Deeds | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds (1872 onward) | In-person |
| NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago) | Post-1906 naturalizations; federal court records | In-person |
| Illinois State Archives (Springfield) | State-level records; 1855 and 1865 state censuses | In-person; some online |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-fire (pre-October 1871) Cook County civil vital records — destroyed, no online equivalent
- Pre-fire Cook County probate and court records — destroyed, no online equivalent
- Pre-fire Cook County deed records — destroyed; reconstructed Burnt Record Act deeds (1872+) are at the Recorder of Deeds, not fully digitized
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society records (fire victims/relief recipients) — at the Chicago History Museum, physical access
- Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance/title records — at the Chicago History Museum, physical access
- Many church parish registers (especially for denominations whose parishes did not survive the fire) — contact denominational archives
- Illinois state census 1855 and 1865 — not fully indexed online; Illinois State Archives
- Cook County sexton and burial records for many cemeteries — contact individual cemeteries

## Known record losses

The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse. According to Wikipedia's article on the fire (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire), this destroyed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. The FamilySearch Wiki's Cook County genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire) confirms that genealogists must use substitute sources for the pre-fire period.

Not all church registers were lost: parishes that kept their registers at the parish house (rather than the courthouse) may have survived. Whether any particular parish's registers survived depends on the parish's location relative to the fire's path and its record-keeping practices — contact the Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives to determine which Catholic parish registers exist and which do not.

The federal census records (1850, 1860, 1870) survived because the originals were held in Washington. BLM General Land Office federal patent records also survived. Post-fire records from late 1871 onward are substantially intact.

## Research tips

- **Start with the 1870 federal census.** It is the last surviving pre-fire census for Chicago and captures families before the disaster. Cross-reference with city directories from the Newberry Library to establish address and occupation. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County genealogy page — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)
- **Search the Chicago Relief and Aid Society records.** After the fire, this organization distributed aid to displaced families and maintained records at the Chicago History Museum naming thousands of recipients. These records are among the few direct sources naming families specifically affected by the fire. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County genealogy — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)
- **Use the Burnt Record Act deeds as a bridge.** Property owners who re-registered under the 1872 Act often recited the history of their property ownership in their re-recorded deed, preserving pre-fire chain-of-title information.
- **Check church registers before and after the fire separately.** A parish that survived may have pre-fire baptism and marriage registers intact; one destroyed in the fire may have reconstructed its register from memory in the months after. Contact the Archdiocese archives for the status of each parish.
- **Civil War pension files can substitute for destroyed vital records.** If a family member served in the Civil War, his pension file will contain sworn affidavits about birth date and place, marriage date and place, and children — all of which are invaluable substitutes for the records destroyed in 1871.
- **Search German-language newspapers** for immigrant families. Chicago had a substantial German-language press before and after the fire; obituaries and marriage notices appeared there rather than in the Tribune.
- **Fire-era newspaper notices.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of displaced persons and relief recipients in October–November 1871; these can place a family at a specific relief station or temporary address immediately after the fire.
- **Illinois land patents are at the BLM GLO** (https://glorecords.blm.gov) and were not affected by the courthouse fire — original federal land grants are fully intact.

---

## French Colonial Louisiana (1700–1803): Records & Repositories

**Historical context:** Louisiana was governed by France, then Spain (from 1769), then briefly France again before the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. The Catholic Church was the *only* legally recognized institution for recording vital events throughout this period — civil registration did not exist.

---

### Primary Record Type: Catholic Sacramental Registers
- **Baptisms, marriages, and burials** are the core genealogical source
- Registers begin as early as 1720
- Records are in **18th-century French and Spanish** — no name index; must be browsed image-by-image
- Available through FamilySearch (digitized but unindexed volumes)

### Other Key Records
- **Superior Council notarial acts** (from 1699) — also on FamilySearch, unindexed
- **Spanish Cabildo court, estate, and land records**
- **Wills, marriage contracts, property transactions** (from the 1730s)

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council & Spanish Cabildo records, estate and land records |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | Wills, marriage contracts, property transactions from the 1730s |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial administrative records, census rolls, and passenger lists — unique holdings not found elsewhere |

---

### Recommended Next Step
Narrow to a **specific parish or family**, then build a research plan targeting the Catholic registers and Superior Council estate records most likely to document that family. Use the **search-images** agent to browse the unindexed FamilySearch volumes, and consider the **translation** agent for the French and Spanish handwriting.

quirks: Louisiana was under French authority 1699-1762, Spanish authority 1762-1800, and briefly French again 1800-1803 before the Louisiana Purchase. Records and record languages shift accordingly — French before 1769, Spanish from 1769, French again briefly in 1800-1803.

The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. All vital events — for free persons and for enslaved persons under the Code Noir — were registered as Catholic sacramental acts (baptism, marriage, burial), not civil records. Civil registration did not begin until after statehood (1812).

The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) created by France and succeeded by the Spanish Cabildo handled all colonial court, land, contract, and estate business. Its records, held at the Louisiana Historical Center, are the main non-church record set for 1699-1803.
New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.

France transferred the western half of Louisiana to Spain by the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1762, but Spanish administration did not begin until 1769. Records from 1762-1769 may still be in French.

The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence, muster rolls, and census rolls for the French colonial period — an essential repository not accessible through FamilySearch.

The two digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period (DGS 004330991 and 004330992) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image. Records are in French and Spanish — original-language reading skills are required.

The FamilySearch Louisiana-specific wiki pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, Census, Naming Customs) all returned only generic content in this survey — consult the Louisiana Genealogy wiki page directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for jurisdiction-specific guidance.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** France claimed the Mississippi River basin in 1682; permanent settlement began 1699; New Orleans founded 1718.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (capital of the colony throughout the period).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (French crown) 1699–1762; Kingdom of Spain 1762–1800; France briefly 1800–1803.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tools for this period. Colonial censuses do exist (see Census section below).
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, and later sugar cultivation; significant enslaved labor force under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian exiles (arriving from 1755 onward), Spanish administrators (from 1769), free people of color (gens de couleur libres), and a large enslaved African population.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively (only legally recognized church under French and Spanish rule). No other denominations kept legal registers during this period.
- **Key historical events:** French founding 1699–1718; Treaty of Fontainebleau (secret transfer to Spain) 1762; Spanish administration begins 1769; American Revolution period disruptions; retrocession to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- The colony's boundaries were not fixed to modern Louisiana — French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi basin.
- France ceded the western portion (including New Orleans) to Spain by the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1762, but Spanish administration did not begin until 1769. Records from 1762–1769 continue in French under transitional authority.
- France briefly retook the territory in 1800 before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase transferred it to the United States.
- Because the colony predates the U.S. parish (county-equivalent) system, records are organized by administrative post and Catholic parish rather than by modern Louisiana parishes. The modern parish system was imposed after statehood (1812).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist in French colonial Louisiana. The FamilySearch Louisiana-specific Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for authoritative dates.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1700–1803. The Catholic sacramental registers are the functional equivalent — baptisms = births, marriage registers = marriages, burial registers = deaths.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Catholic parish registers are the primary and often sole source for vital events during this entire period (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (legally mandated under French and Spanish colonial law).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, and burials. Confirmation registers exist for some parishes.
- **Enslaved persons:** The Code Noir required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so sacramental registers often name enslaved individuals along with their enslaver — a critical source for researching enslaved ancestry.
- **Earliest registers:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans, has registers from 1720.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — this is an indexed collection covering from 1718.
- **Digitized volumes (FamilySearch):** Volume DGS 004330991 (264 images) covers sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803. Records are in **French and Spanish**. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. Reading the original French and Spanish is required.
- **Language:** French throughout the French period (to 1769); Spanish from 1769 onward under Spanish administration, with French continuing in some parishes.
- **Where held:** Originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and at the Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans). FamilySearch holds microfilmed/digitized copies.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France conducted several census enumerations of the Louisiana colony (recensements), including one circa 1699–1700 and others in the early 18th century. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, and have been partially published.
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was not part of the United States until 1803 (Louisiana Purchase) and did not achieve statehood until 1812. No federal census covers this territory during the 1700–1803 period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM (physical and partially digitized via the ANOM online portal at anom.archivesdefrance.culture.gouv.fr). The FamilySearch Louisiana Census wiki page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for published transcriptions.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, successions, guardianships, contracts — all handled by the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) under French rule and by the Spanish Cabildo under Spanish rule.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — this indexed collection begins in 1756 and covers the colonial period.
- **Digitized volumes (FamilySearch):** Volume DGS 004330992 (149 images) covers French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records, 1699–1769. Records are in **French and Spanish**. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse-only. Reading the original language is required.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans) holds the Superior Council and Cabildo records. These have been partially digitized. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial acts from the 1730s onward (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants per the FamilySearch Wiki search result).

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The French crown (through the Superior Council) granted concessions (land grants) to colonists. Under Spanish rule, the system shifted to Spanish land grants (merced). After the Louisiana Purchase, existing French and Spanish grants were adjudicated under U.S. law.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts of sale, mortgage records.
- **Key repositories:** French and Spanish colonial grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series (published, widely available). Original notarial records are at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access). The Louisiana State Land Office holds some records. ANOM holds administrative land correspondence.
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpent strips fronting waterways), not the U.S. rectangular survey system — boundaries described by natural features and arpent measurements.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian wars, the Seven Years' War (ending in cession to Spain 1762), American Revolution (Spain as an ally), and border skirmishes throughout.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, troop lists, officer commissions, pension correspondence.
- **Where held:** ANOM in Aix-en-Provence holds French colonial military records. The Spanish military records for Louisiana are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain. Some have been microfilmed. NARA holds records for the brief U.S. territorial period after 1803. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized military records but coverage of the French colonial period is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (established 1789, under Spanish rule) is the oldest surviving cemetery. Earlier burials were in churchyard grounds.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some entries for colonial-era burials, but coverage is sparse for the 1700s.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers (where they survive) are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in Louisiana during the French colonial period. The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, appeared in 1794 (under Spanish rule).
- **Where held:** Early issues of the Moniteur de la Louisiane are held at Tulane University's Howard-Tilton Memorial Library and at the Louisiana State Museum. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has minimal coverage for this early period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout this period.
- **Record types:** French colonial ship passenger lists (passports for travel to the colony), engagés (indentured servant contracts), Acadian exile lists (1755 onward).
- **Where held:** ANOM holds French colonial embarkation lists and passenger records. The Spanish colonial equivalents are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). The Acadian exile records have been extensively published and are accessible through the Council for the Development of French in Louisiana (CODOFIL) and through published works such as those by Donald Hébert.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including family units — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family's arrival.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Capitation (head tax) and property assessments under both French and Spanish colonial administrations.
- **Date range:** French colonial tax lists are fragmentary and held primarily at ANOM. Spanish-era tax records (from 1769) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center and at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls (see Census section) overlap with tax lists in naming heads of household with property and family composition.

### Other record types

French colonial Louisiana (1700-1803) was governed first by France, then Spain (from 1769), then briefly France again before the Louisiana Purchase. All vital events — for free persons and for enslaved persons under the Code Noir — were registered as Catholic sacramental acts (baptism, marriage, burial), not civil records. Civil registration did not begin until after statehood (1812).

The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) created by France and succeeded by the Spanish Cabildo handled all colonial court, land, contract, and estate business. Its records, held at the Louisiana Historical Center, are the main non-church record set for 1699-1803.
New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.

France transferred the western half of Louisiana to Spain by the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1762, but Spanish administration did not begin until 1769. Records from 1762-1769 may still be in French.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** France claimed the Mississippi River basin in 1682; permanent settlement began 1699; New Orleans founded 1718.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (capital of the colony throughout the period).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (French crown) 1699–1762; Kingdom of Spain 1762–1800; France briefly 1800–1803.
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tools for this period. Colonial censuses do exist (see Census section below).
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo, tobacco, and later sugar cultivation; significant enslaved labor force under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, Acadian exiles (arriving from 1755 onward), Spanish administrators (from 1769), free people of color (gens de couleur libres), and a large enslaved African population.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively (only legally recognized church under French and Spanish rule). No other denominations kept legal registers during this period.
- **Key historical events:** French founding 1699–1718; Treaty of Fontainebleau (secret transfer to Spain) 1762; Spanish administration begins 1769; American Revolution period disruptions; retrocession to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- The colony's boundaries were not fixed to modern Louisiana — French Louisiana encompassed the entire Mississippi basin.
- France ceded the western portion (including New Orleans) to Spain by the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1762, but Spanish administration did not begin until 1769. Records from 1762–1769 continue in French under transitional authority.
- France briefly retook the territory in 1800 before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase transferred it to the United States.
- Because the colony predates the U.S. parish (county-equivalent) system, records are organized by administrative post and Catholic parish rather than by modern Louisiana parishes. The modern parish system was imposed after statehood (1812).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration did not exist in French colonial Louisiana. The FamilySearch Louisiana-specific Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for authoritative dates.
- **What exists:** No civil vital records for 1700–1803. The Catholic sacramental registers are the functional equivalent — baptisms = births, marriage registers = marriages, burial registers = deaths.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Catholic parish registers are the primary and often sole source for vital events during this entire period (see Church Records below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (legally mandated under French and Spanish colonial law).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, and burials. Confirmation registers exist for some parishes.
- **Enslaved persons:** The Code Noir required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so sacramental registers often name enslaved individuals along with their enslaver — a critical source for researching enslaved ancestry.
- **Earliest registers:** St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans, has registers from 1720.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — this is an indexed collection covering from 1718.
- **Digitized volumes (FamilySearch):** Volume DGS 004330991 (264 images) covers sacramental registers of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803. Records are in **French and Spanish**. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. Reading the original French and Spanish is required.
- **Language:** French throughout the French period (to 1769); Spanish from 1769 onward under Spanish administration, with French continuing in some parishes.
- **Where held:** Originals at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and at the Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans). FamilySearch holds microfilmed/digitized copies.

### Census records
- **Colonial censuses:** France conducted several census enumerations of the Louisiana colony (recensements), including one circa 1699–1700 and others in the early 18th century. These are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, and have been partially published.
- **Federal census:** Louisiana was not part of the United States until 1803 (Louisiana Purchase) and did not achieve statehood until 1812. No federal census covers this territory during the 1700–1803 period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM (physical and partially digitized via the ANOM online portal at anom.archivesdefrance.culture.gouv.fr). The FamilySearch Louisiana Census wiki page returned only generic content — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy for published transcriptions.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, successions, guardianships, contracts — all handled by the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) under French rule and by the Spanish Cabildo under Spanish rule.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection 2078341, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — this indexed collection begins in 1756 and covers the colonial period.
- **Digitized volumes (FamilySearch):** Volume DGS 004330992 (149 images) covers French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records, 1699–1769. Records are in **French and Spanish**. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse-only. Reading the original language is required.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans) holds the Superior Council and Cabildo records. These have been partially digitized. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial acts from the 1730s onward (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants per the FamilySearch Wiki search result).

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The French crown (through the Superior Council) granted concessions (land grants) to colonists. Under Spanish rule, the system shifted to Spanish land grants (merced). After the Louisiana Purchase, existing French and Spanish grants were adjudicated under U.S. law.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts of sale, mortgage records.
- **Key repositories:** French and Spanish colonial grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series (published, widely available). Original notarial records are at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access). The Louisiana State Land Office holds some records. ANOM holds administrative land correspondence.
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpent strips fronting waterways), not the U.S. rectangular survey system — boundaries described by natural features and arpent measurements.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian wars, the Seven Years' War (ending in cession to Spain 1762), American Revolution (Spain as an ally), and border skirmishes throughout.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, troop lists, officer commissions, pension correspondence.
- **Where held:** ANOM in Aix-en-Provence holds French colonial military records. The Spanish military records for Louisiana are at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, Spain. Some have been microfilmed. NARA holds records for the brief U.S. territorial period after 1803. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) holds some digitized military records but coverage of the French colonial period is limited.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans (established 1789, under Spanish rule) is the oldest surviving cemetery. Earlier burials were in churchyard grounds.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some entries for colonial-era burials, but coverage is sparse for the 1700s.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers (where they survive) are held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in Louisiana during the French colonial period. The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, appeared in 1794 (under Spanish rule).
- **Where held:** Early issues of the Moniteur de la Louisiane are held at Tulane University's Howard-Tilton Memorial Library and at the Louisiana State Museum. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has minimal coverage for this early period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for the colony throughout this period.
- **Record types:** French colonial ship passenger lists (passports for travel to the colony), engagés (indentured servant contracts), Acadian exile lists (1755 onward).
- **Where held:** ANOM holds French colonial embarkation lists and passenger records. The Spanish colonial equivalents are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). The Acadian exile records have been extensively published and are accessible through the Council for the Development of French in Louisiana (CODOFIL) and through published works such as those by Donald Hébert.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard including family units — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family's arrival.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Capitation (head tax) and property assessments under both French and Spanish colonial administrations.
- **Date range:** French colonial tax lists are fragmentary and held primarily at ANOM. Spanish-era tax records (from 1769) are held at the Louisiana Historical Center and at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls (see Census section) overlap with tax lists in naming heads of household with property and family composition.

### Other record types
- **Notarial acts:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, apprenticeships, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. These are among the richest sources for colonial-period family and social history and are accessible to the public at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
- **Slave records:** The Code Noir required documentation of the baptism, marriage, and manumission of enslaved persons. These appear in Catholic sacramental registers and in notarial acts (bills of sale, manumission documents). The Louisiana Historical Center holds slave records as part of the Superior Council/Cabildo archives.
- **Published colonial records and transcriptions:** A number of colonial records have been transcribed and published — notably by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society and in Donald Hébert's multi-volume *South Louisiana Records*. These are finding aids and transcription projects, not original records.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from parts of Berks County and Northampton County
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query; no figures are available from tool results.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; the county was the heart of the southern anthracite coal fields. Related industries included iron foundries, colliery supply businesses, and railroads (particularly the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad).
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish Catholic community (particularly post-1840s Famine immigration); Welsh miners (Congregationalist and Baptist); later waves of Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants from the 1880s onward.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Reformed.
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires activity and trials (1870s); formation of the United Mine Workers of America (1890); repeated labor strikes; major mine accidents throughout the period.

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. Records of events before 1811 for places now in Schuylkill County will be found in those parent counties.
- Boundaries were stable throughout the 1840–1910 target period.
- Neighboring coal counties Luzerne and Lackawanna are relevant: Lackawanna County was formed from Luzerne County in 1878. Records for places now in Lackawanna County that predate 1878 were filed under Luzerne County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only a generic page and do not state a specific earlier local or county-level registration date for Schuylkill County; the 1906 statewide date is the confirmed registration threshold from tool results.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317; 4,218,763 indexed records with images) covers Patrick Flynn's 1908 death. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317; 524,189 records) and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957; 312,045 records) cover marriages in the period. Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909; 198,765 records, no images) covers earlier marriages by compilation.
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch (collections above). Physical originals of post-1906 certificates at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration before 1906 at the statewide level. For births and deaths 1840–1905, church records and census mortality schedules are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal registers, census mortality schedules (1850–1880), newspaper death notices, cemetery sexton records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separately dated event, years after baptism). For Irish Catholic families in particular, baptismal registers are the primary birth evidence before 1906.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; 1,245,830 records; images covering 1708–1985) is available online at FamilySearch. Physical registers remain at individual parishes or have been transferred to diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill County parishes). The Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) holds transcriptions and some originals.
- **Language:** English for most denominations; Latin for Roman Catholic sacramental entries; Welsh for Welsh-language congregations.
- **Note:** Ethnic parishes served specific mining communities and are not interchangeable — an Irish Catholic miner's family will appear in the Irish parish, not a generic county register. Identify which parish served the specific mining town before searching. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 all cover Schuylkill County. (1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationally.) Occupation is listed — 'miner' identifies coal mining families throughout 1870–1900 censuses.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850–1880, listing deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration — a critical pre-1906 death source.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1850–1880 and 1900–1910 are indexed and available online at FamilySearch, Ancestry (subscription), and other platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Also: naturalization petitions (pre-1906 naturalizations filed in the Court of Common Pleas).
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1811.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196; 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records — browse-only). Physical originals at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Naturalization note:** Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, so also check federal court records. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania issued warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's land office. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original warrant and patent books. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only a generic page; specific details of the county deed recorder's holdings were not confirmed by tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. Mining families in the coal region often appear in deeds as lessees of company-owned land (many miners rented rather than owned).
- **Where held:** Deed records at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; tax records at the county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) and Spanish-American War (1898) fall within or near the target period. Men born ca. 1845 (like Patrick Flynn) would have been of draft age during the Civil War.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (NARA); Civil War draft registrations (1863, Consolidated Lists); Molly Maguires-era court records may also name individuals.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for military records online; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Schuylkill County has numerous Catholic, Protestant, and municipal cemeteries in mining towns (Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Ashland, Minersville).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Schuylkill County cemetery entries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries or church parishes; some transcribed by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville), published from 1825, is the principal regional newspaper; it contains death notices, marriage announcements, mine accident reports, and legal notices throughout the target period.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania State Library; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pennsylvania newspapers including mining-region titles.
- **Content value:** Obituaries often contain Irish birthplace information and names of surviving relatives — critical for immigrants who left no other paper trail before 1906.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary for Irish and later eastern European arrivals) and New York (Castle Garden pre-1892; Ellis Island 1892–1957).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests, declarations of intention (first papers), petitions for naturalization, Certificate of Arrival forms (post-1906).
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry U.S. Federal Census Collection and passenger list databases. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) specifically at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Post-1895 manifests list last residence in origin country and a contact in the U.S. — both valuable for tracing Irish or eastern European origins. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Occupational records (coal mining — unique to this region)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (DGS 002240015):** 410 images; 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable; covers Schuylkill County 1870–1900. This is the single most searchable mining-specific record in the tool results.
- **State Mine Inspector reports:** Published annually from 1870; list fatal accidents with name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and some libraries. Not confirmed as digitized online by tool results.
- **Company employment records:** Payrolls and accident reports survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA records:** United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files. The Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) holds local mining collections. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment records.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives holds some series. Tax records substitute usefully for the destroyed 1890 federal census.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1708–1985 (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, browse-only); Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317, indexed); County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317, indexed); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957, indexed); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909, indexed, no images); Mine Worker Employment Cards 1870–1900 (DGS 002240015, 95% indexed + full-text) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers including Miners' Journal | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, military pension files | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes matching this place and period; only the first page (3 volumes) was examined. A nextPageToken (PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) is present, indicating 20 additional volumes were not reviewed. The three examined volumes are: Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill 1870–1900 (DGS 002240015; 95% indexed + full-text searchable); Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne 1870–1895 (DGS 002240016; browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna 1878–1900 (DGS 002240017; browse-only).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA | Deeds, probate, court records including pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person or mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Statewide vital records (post-1906), naturalization records (1840s–1906), state mine records, land warrants | In-person or online request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville, PA | Local newspapers (Miners' Journal), cemetery transcriptions, local histories, coal company records | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton, PA | UMWA records, mining company collections, ethnic community records | In-person |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County | Contact archives |
| Denominational archives (Welsh Congregational, etc.) | Welsh and other Protestant parish registers | Contact respective archives |

## Records NOT online
- **Birth records before 1906:** No statewide civil birth registration existed; births are documented only in church baptismal registers, many of which are physical-only at parishes or diocesan archives.
- **Death records before 1906:** Same gap; substitutes are church burial registers, census mortality schedules (1850–1880), and newspaper notices.
- **State Mine Inspector reports (1870+):** Not confirmed as digitized; available physically at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Company payroll and employment records (beyond DGS 002240015):** Survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies — physical access required.
- **UMWA membership rolls and grievance files:** Held at the Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton — physical access.
- **County tax assessment records:** Physical at the county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **20 of the 23 digitized volumes identified by volume_search:** Not yet reviewed; the next page of results (token PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) was not fetched.

## Known record losses
No specific courthouse fire or record destruction for Schuylkill County was stated in any tool result returned for this survey. The 1890 federal census is destroyed nationally — tax records and state mine records are the primary substitutes for that year for this county. No tool result confirmed or denied the survival of any specific parish's registers; researchers should contact individual parish offices or the Diocese of Allentown Archives to confirm holdings before assuming records are lost.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the most important pre-1906 vital source.** Identify the specific ethnic parish for the mining town where your ancestor lived — Irish Catholic families in Schuylkill County will appear in Irish Catholic parish registers, not in a merged county index. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **The Mine Worker Employment Cards (DGS 002240015) are 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — search these first for any male ancestor in Schuylkill County 1870–1900 before turning to browse-only volumes.
- **State Mine Inspector reports (annual from 1870) list fatal accidents** with name, age, nationality, and cause of death — an irreplaceable source if an ancestor died in a mine accident. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **For immigration origins:** Post-1895 passenger manifests list the last residence in the origin country and a U.S. contact. Naturalization records (first papers filed in Schuylkill County courts, 1840s–1906, at Pennsylvania State Archives) often state birthplace and arrival date. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Use the 1880 census mortality schedule and newspaper notices** as death evidence for 1840–1905 events — particularly the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, from 1825), which published death notices and accident reports throughout the period.
- **Search adjoining counties.** Mining families moved between Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties following work. Note: Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne in 1878 — records for places now in Lackawanna that predate 1878 were filed under Luzerne County.
- **The Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville)** hold collections not available online, including UMWA records and local coal company archives. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Land Records, Probate, Census, and Naming Customs** all returned only a generic fallback page during this survey rather than Pennsylvania-specific content; researchers should consult them directly at familysearch.org/wiki for the most current guidance.
