The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records returned only a generic page and do not state a specific earlier local or county-level registration date for Schuylkill County; the 1906 statewide date is the confirmed registration threshold from tool results.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317; 4,218,763 indexed records with images) covers Patrick Flynn's 1908 death. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317; 524,189 records) and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957; 312,045 records) cover marriages in the period. Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (collection 1502909; 198,765 records, no images) covers earlier marriages by compilation.
- **Where held:** Online at FamilySearch (collections above). Physical originals of post-1906 certificates at the Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration before 1906 at the statewide level. For births and deaths 1840–1905, church records and census mortality schedules are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal registers, census mortality schedules (1850–1880), newspaper death notices, cemetery sexton records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak), Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Reformed.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separately dated event, years after baptism). For Irish Catholic families in particular, baptismal registers are the primary birth evidence before 1906.
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; 1,245,830 records; images covering 1708–1985) is available online at FamilySearch. Physical registers remain at individual parishes or have been transferred to diocesan archives (Diocese of Allentown for Schuylkill County parishes). The Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) holds transcriptions and some originals.
- **Language:** English for most denominations; Latin for Roman Catholic sacramental entries; Welsh for Welsh-language congregations.
- **Note:** Ethnic parishes served specific mining communities and are not interchangeable — an Irish Catholic miner's family will appear in the Irish parish, not a generic county register. Identify which parish served the specific mining town before searching. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 all cover Schuylkill County. (1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationally.) Occupation is listed — 'miner' identifies coal mining families throughout 1870–1900 censuses.
- **Mortality schedules:** Available 1850–1880, listing deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration — a critical pre-1906 death source.
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state census during this period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses 1850–1880 and 1900–1910 are indexed and available online at FamilySearch, Ancestry (subscription), and other platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Also: naturalization petitions (pre-1906 naturalizations filed in the Court of Common Pleas).
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1811.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (collection 1999196; 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records — browse-only). Physical originals at the Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Naturalization note:** Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, so also check federal court records. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania issued warrants and patents through the Commonwealth's land office. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original warrant and patent books. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property returned only a generic page; specific details of the county deed recorder's holdings were not confirmed by tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records. Mining families in the coal region often appear in deeds as lessees of company-owned land (many miners rented rather than owned).
- **Where held:** Deed records at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville; tax records at the county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) and Spanish-American War (1898) fall within or near the target period. Men born ca. 1845 (like Patrick Flynn) would have been of draft age during the Civil War.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records and pension files (NARA); Civil War draft registrations (1863, Consolidated Lists); Molly Maguires-era court records may also name individuals.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for military records online; Pennsylvania State Archives for state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Schuylkill County has numerous Catholic, Protestant, and municipal cemeteries in mining towns (Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Ashland, Minersville).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many Schuylkill County cemetery entries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries or church parishes; some transcribed by the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Miners' Journal (Pottsville), published from 1825, is the principal regional newspaper; it contains death notices, marriage announcements, mine accident reports, and legal notices throughout the target period.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania State Library; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has historical Pennsylvania newspapers including mining-region titles.
- **Content value:** Obituaries often contain Irish birthplace information and names of surviving relatives — critical for immigrants who left no other paper trail before 1906.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia (primary for Irish and later eastern European arrivals) and New York (Castle Garden pre-1892; Ellis Island 1892–1957).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests, declarations of intention (first papers), petitions for naturalization, Certificate of Arrival forms (post-1906).
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Ancestry U.S. Federal Census Collection and passenger list databases. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) specifically at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Post-1895 manifests list last residence in origin country and a contact in the U.S. — both valuable for tracing Irish or eastern European origins. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Occupational records (coal mining — unique to this region)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (DGS 002240015):** 410 images; 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable; covers Schuylkill County 1870–1900. This is the single most searchable mining-specific record in the tool results.
- **State Mine Inspector reports:** Published annually from 1870; list fatal accidents with name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Available at the Pennsylvania State Archives and some libraries. Not confirmed as digitized online by tool results.
- **Company employment records:** Payrolls and accident reports survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA records:** United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files. The Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) holds local mining collections. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax and personal property assessment records.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1811).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives holds some series. Tax records substitute usefully for the destroyed 1890 federal census.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1708–1985 (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); Probate Records 1683–1994 (1999196, browse-only); Death Certificates 1906–1968 (2255317, indexed); County Marriages 1885–1950 (1921317, indexed); Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (1571957, indexed); Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (1502909, indexed, no images); Mine Worker Employment Cards 1870–1900 (DGS 002240015, 95% indexed + full-text) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers including Miners' Journal | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, military pension files | Free / fee for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes matching this place and period; only the first page (3 volumes) was examined. A nextPageToken (PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) is present, indicating 20 additional volumes were not reviewed. The three examined volumes are: Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill 1870–1900 (DGS 002240015; 95% indexed + full-text searchable); Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne 1870–1895 (DGS 002240016; browse-only); Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna 1878–1900 (DGS 002240017; browse-only).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA | Deeds, probate, court records including pre-1906 naturalizations | In-person or mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | Statewide vital records (post-1906), naturalization records (1840s–1906), state mine records, land warrants | In-person or online request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County, Pottsville, PA | Local newspapers (Miners' Journal), cemetery transcriptions, local histories, coal company records | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton, PA | UMWA records, mining company collections, ethnic community records | In-person |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County | Contact archives |
| Denominational archives (Welsh Congregational, etc.) | Welsh and other Protestant parish registers | Contact respective archives |

## Records NOT online
- **Birth records before 1906:** No statewide civil birth registration existed; births are documented only in church baptismal registers, many of which are physical-only at parishes or diocesan archives.
- **Death records before 1906:** Same gap; substitutes are church burial registers, census mortality schedules (1850–1880), and newspaper notices.
- **State Mine Inspector reports (1870+):** Not confirmed as digitized; available physically at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Company payroll and employment records (beyond DGS 002240015):** Survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies — physical access required.
- **UMWA membership rolls and grievance files:** Held at the Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton — physical access.
- **County tax assessment records:** Physical at the county courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **20 of the 23 digitized volumes identified by volume_search:** Not yet reviewed; the next page of results (token PA_COAL_REGION_PAGE_2) was not fetched.

## Known record losses
No specific courthouse fire or record destruction for Schuylkill County was stated in any tool result returned for this survey. The 1890 federal census is destroyed nationally — tax records and state mine records are the primary substitutes for that year for this county. No tool result confirmed or denied the survival of any specific parish's registers; researchers should contact individual parish offices or the Diocese of Allentown Archives to confirm holdings before assuming records are lost.

## Research tips
- **Church records are the most important pre-1906 vital source.** Identify the specific ethnic parish for the mining town where your ancestor lived — Irish Catholic families in Schuylkill County will appear in Irish Catholic parish registers, not in a merged county index. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **The Mine Worker Employment Cards (DGS 002240015) are 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — search these first for any male ancestor in Schuylkill County 1870–1900 before turning to browse-only volumes.
- **State Mine Inspector reports (annual from 1870) list fatal accidents** with name, age, nationality, and cause of death — an irreplaceable source if an ancestor died in a mine accident. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **For immigration origins:** Post-1895 passenger manifests list the last residence in the origin country and a U.S. contact. Naturalization records (first papers filed in Schuylkill County courts, 1840s–1906, at Pennsylvania State Archives) often state birthplace and arrival date. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Use the 1880 census mortality schedule and newspaper notices** as death evidence for 1840–1905 events — particularly the Miners' Journal (Pottsville, from 1825), which published death notices and accident reports throughout the period.
- **Search adjoining counties.** Mining families moved between Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties following work. Note: Lackawanna County formed from Luzerne in 1878 — records for places now in Lackawanna that predate 1878 were filed under Luzerne County.
- **The Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville)** hold collections not available online, including UMWA records and local coal company archives. ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Land Records, Probate, Census, and Naming Customs** all returned only a generic fallback page during this survey rather than Pennsylvania-specific content; researchers should consult them directly at familysearch.org/wiki for the most current guidance.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Early Massachusetts (1620–1700) is exceptionally well-documented by colonial standards. The colony mandated that every town record births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639** — one of the earliest such laws in North America — and Congregational (Puritan) church registers, county probate courts, deed registries, and colonial court minutes have survived in remarkably complete runs.

**Key repositories:**
- **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) — colonial-era court, legislative, and vital records
- **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** — the premier resource; holds the *Great Migration* study series, essential for pre-1643 arrivals
- **Individual town clerk offices** — original town vital records
- **County courthouses** — probate and deed records
- **FamilySearch** — many records indexed or available as browsable images

**Important distinction:** Before 1691, there were **two separate colonies** — **Plymouth Colony** and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** — each with its own court and record series. You must identify which colony your ancestor's town belonged to before searching.

**For arrivals before 1643:** The *Great Migration* study series at NEHGS is the essential starting point and cannot be replaced by online sources alone.

To build a focused research plan, the next step would be narrowing to a **specific town** and confirming whether it fell under Plymouth or Massachusetts Bay — that determines which record series to target first.

args.query: Massachusetts early colonial Puritan settlement genealogy records 1600s
Massachusetts Bay Colony Puritan settlement 1620s 1630s history

quirks: The colony (and later Province) did NOT use counties as the primary record-keeping unit in the earliest decades — vital events were recorded at the town level. Always research by town, not by county.

Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) kept records separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691); after their 1691 merger into the Province of Massachusetts Bay, records continue under the province. Search both colony-era record sets for the pre-1691 period.

Massachusetts mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1639 — one of the earliest such mandates in North America. Town vital records are therefore available from that date at the town level, not a county or state level.
No statewide civil vital registration existed in this period; all vital recording was at the town level from 1639.

The Congregational (Puritan) Church was the established church of the colony. Congregational church records — baptisms, marriages, burials, membership admissions, disciplinary actions — are essential primary sources and often predate or supplement town records.
The 'Great Migration' study series (New England Historic Genealogical Society) documents every known settler arriving 1620-1643 and is the premier finding aid for these earliest families.
The multi-volume 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is a critical index for the colonial period.

FamilySearch digitized 2 volumes covering 1620-1700: one of town meeting and proprietors' records (DGS 007612044, 188 images, browse-only, not name-indexed) and one of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed). Both must be browsed or full-text searched; neither has a name index.

Federal census records begin only in 1790 — there are no federal censuses for the colonial period. Substitute sources include colonial muster rolls, tax lists, church membership lists, and town proprietors' records.

Land records (deeds, grants) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts.
The Massachusetts Archives in Boston holds original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward — many not yet digitized.

New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) in Boston has the largest genealogical research library in New England, including manuscript collections, published genealogies, and Great Migration studies.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628; merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691
- **Administrative centers:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown (colonial charter); Province of Massachusetts Bay after 1691
- **Population during period:** Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived 1630-1640 in the Great Migration (Wikipedia, Massachusetts Bay Colony). By 1700 the combined colonial population was roughly 55,000-70,000.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, timber, fur trade, early maritime commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; some Dutch and other European minorities; Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and others)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (Puritan) — the established church; small numbers of Anglicans, Quakers (tolerated after 1661 under pressure), Baptists, and other dissenters

- **1628-1630:** Massachusetts Bay Colony established — governed the area around Boston and the rest of present Massachusetts.
- **1643:** New England Confederation formed, linking Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut, and New Haven colonies; did not change internal record-keeping jurisdiction.
- **1691:** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay by royal charter. Records from each colony continue as predecessors; after 1691, the province's records are unified.

- **Colonial-era substitutes:** Town proprietors' lists, militia/muster rolls, church membership lists, and colonial tax lists serve as population proxies. ### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. County probate courts operated from the 1630s.
- **Date range:** Probate records begin in the 1630s. FamilySearch collection **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991** (collection 1678901, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) covers the colonial period.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (the relevant counties for 1620-1700 are Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Plymouth, and Bristol). (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Massachusetts Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational; wiki_search result citing Massachusetts Archives)
- **Court records:** The General Court (colonial legislature) and county courts generated minutes naming ordinary colonists in property disputes, land grants, criminal cases, and colonial assessments. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) is the primary repository for these.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England system; no rectangular survey)

### Military records

- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the colonial period are rare; most evidence comes from surviving gravestones and published transcriptions.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Colonial tax lists, town rates (assessments)
- **Date range:** Colonial tax lists survive from the 1640s-1650s in many towns, though coverage is uneven.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) and individual town archives. Some have been published or transcribed.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (coll. 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (coll. 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (coll. 1678901); DGS 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors' records, browse-only); DGS 007612045 (Suffolk Co. Congregational admissions/baptisms, full-text searchable) | Free |
| Ancestry | Vital records, church records, probate, and land record compilations for Massachusetts | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Colonial burying ground gravestone transcriptions | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Some colonial-era Massachusetts records; more relevant post-1776 | Free/fee for copies |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives (Boston) | Original colony records, General Court minutes, court records, governor's correspondence from 1620s onward; colonial militia records; tax lists | In-person; some records available via microfilm or published transcriptions |

| County Probate Courts | Probate files from the 1630s onward | In-person; digitized via FamilySearch |

- Colonial tax lists are largely unpublished or available only in physical form at the Massachusetts Archives or individual town archives.
- County deed books for the 1630s-1700 are largely microfilm only (FamilySearch library) or physical at the registries.

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic colony-wide record loss is identified in the tool results for this period. Massachusetts has exceptionally complete colonial records by North American standards.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed a number of frontier towns and may have caused localized record losses for those communities. If your ancestor's town was destroyed in the war, surviving records may be fragmentary.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts-specific record types returned only generic content in this survey, so specific loss events at individual repositories cannot be confirmed from tool results. Consult the Massachusetts Archives directly for any known gaps.

## Research tips
- **Town first, always.** Vital records were kept at the town level from 1639. Start with the specific town where your ancestor lived; searching at the county level alone will miss the town vital series. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Massachusetts Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Know which colony the town belonged to.** For any event before 1691, determine whether the town was in Plymouth Colony or Massachusetts Bay Colony — the record series are separate. After 1691, both are under the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **Start with the Great Migration series.** For any ancestor who may have arrived before 1643, the Great Migration study series (NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org) is the premier compiled source, with full documentation of every known settler.
- **Use the Tanner-Corbin series as a finding aid.** The multi-volume 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series abstracts town clerk records for over 200 towns and is widely held in genealogical libraries. It is a critical index before turning to original records.
- **Congregational church records are primary sources, not just supplements.** As the established church, Congregational meetings often recorded events that the town clerk also recorded — but they also captured members who moved between towns, were disciplined, or whose civil records are lost. Neither has a name index — plan to examine every image in the relevant date range.
- **Consult NEHGS in Boston.** For Puritan-era ancestors, NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org) is indispensable. Its manuscript collections, the NEHGS Register (the oldest genealogical journal in America), and the Great Migration series are not fully replicated anywhere online for free.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Massachusetts Bay Colony shared borders with Plymouth Colony (merged 1691), Connecticut Colony, Rhode Island Colony, and New Hampshire. Families near these borders generated records in multiple colonial jurisdictions. Search neighboring colonial records if your ancestor lived near these borders.

| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; NEHGS Register journal | In-person; some holdings online via AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |
| County Registries of Deeds (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Plymouth, Bristol) | Deed books from the 1630s onward | In-person; some records microfilmed/digitized |
| County Probate Courts | Probate files from the 1630s onward | In-person; digitized via FamilySearch |
| Individual town clerk offices | Original town vital records from 1639 | In-person; abstracted in Tanner-Corbin series |
| Local church archives and denominational repositories | Congregational church registers | Varies by congregation |

## Records NOT online
- Most Massachusetts Archives colonial court and legislative records are physical only — not yet digitized.
- Individual town meeting minutes beyond the FamilySearch digitized volume are largely physical or microfilm only.
- Many Congregational church registers outside Suffolk County are not fully digitized — consult NEHGS and church archives directly.
- Colonial tax lists are largely unpublished or available only in physical form at the Massachusetts Archives or individual town archives.
- County deed books for the 1630s-1700 are largely microfilm only (FamilySearch library) or physical at the registries.

## Known record losses
- No catastrophic colony-wide record loss is identified in the tool results for this period. Massachusetts has exceptionally complete colonial records by North American standards.
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed a number of frontier towns and may have caused localized record losses for those communities. If your ancestor's town was destroyed in the war, surviving records may be fragmentary.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts-specific record types returned only generic content in this survey, so specific loss events at individual repositories cannot be confirmed from tool results. Consult the Massachusetts Archives directly for any known gaps.

## Research tips
- **Town first, always.** Vital records were kept at the town level from 1639. Start with the specific town where your ancestor lived; searching at the county level alone will miss the town vital series. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Massachusetts Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records)
- **Know which colony the town belonged to.** For any event before 1691, determine whether the town was in Plymouth Colony or Massachusetts Bay Colony — the record series are separate. After 1691, both are under the Province of Massachusetts Bay.
- **Start with the Great Migration series.** For any ancestor who may have arrived before 1643, the Great Migration study series (NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org) is the premier compiled source, with full documentation of every known settler.
- **Use the Tanner-Corbin series as a finding aid.** The multi-volume 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series abstracts town clerk records for over 200 towns and is widely held in genealogical libraries. It is a critical index before turning to original records.
- **Congregational church records are primary sources, not just supplements.** As the established church, Congregational meetings often recorded events that the town clerk also recorded — but they also captured members who moved between towns, were disciplined, or whose civil records are lost. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Massachusetts Church Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)
- **No colonial-era newspapers.** The first continuous newspaper in Boston did not begin until 1704. Do not expect to find 17th-century obituaries or marriage notices in newspaper databases.
- **Browse-only digitized volumes require patience.** Both FamilySearch-digitized volumes for 1620-1700 require browsing image by image (the town meeting volume, DGS 007612044) or full-text search (the Suffolk Co. church volume, DGS 007612045). Neither has a name index — plan to examine every image in the relevant date range.
- **Consult NEHGS in Boston.** For Puritan-era ancestors, NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org) is indispensable. Its manuscript collections, the NEHGS Register (the oldest genealogical journal in America), and the Great Migration series are not fully replicated anywhere online for free.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** Massachusetts Bay Colony shared borders with Plymouth Colony (merged 1691), Connecticut Colony, Rhode Island Colony, and New Hampshire. Families near these borders generated records in multiple colonial jurisdictions. Search neighboring colonial records if your ancestor lived near these borders.

Locality guide written as **loc_001** in research.json.

---

Oklahoma during the Land Run era (1889–1910) presents a **two-jurisdiction research challenge**: the Unassigned Lands opened in April 1889 were governed as **Oklahoma Territory** from May 1890 until statehood in 1907, while **Indian Territory** — covering the eastern half of present-day Oklahoma, governed by the Five Civilized Tribes — ran an entirely parallel record system until the two merged at statehood.

## Key Records & Repositories

**Homestead Files (BLM/NARA)**
- The most distinctive record for Land Run families is the **federal homestead file**, held at the National Archives (Record Group 49) and partially searchable on [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) and at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov).
- Each file typically contains: the application, five-year proof of residence with **named witnesses**, and the final land patent — one of the richest single documents for a settler family.

**Census Records**
- The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide, but the **Oklahoma Historical Society** holds a rare **1890 special territorial census** covering at least part of the early settler population.
- County **tax rolls from the 1890s** serve as a further substitute.
- The **1900 federal census** is the first fully intact national census after the Land Run and is fully indexed on FamilySearch.

**Tribal Records (Indian Territory families)**
- The **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** (1898–1910) are on FamilySearch but must be browsed image by image — no name index exists.
- These are essential for any family with tribal connections to the Five Civilized Tribes.

**County Records**
- County **marriage records from 1890 onward** are name-indexed on FamilySearch.
- Civil birth and death registration for the territorial period is uncertain — verify directly with the **Oklahoma State Archives** or **State Department of Health** before assuming those records exist.

## Recommended Repositories
| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| National Archives (RG 49) | Homestead case files |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents, online search |
| Oklahoma Historical Society | 1890 territorial census, county records |
| Oklahoma State Archives | Vital records, territorial government records |
| FamilySearch | Homestead files, Dawes rolls, county marriages, 1900 census |

## Next Steps
Identify which **county** (and which territory — Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory) your specific ancestor settled in, then run a focused search in homestead files, the 1890 territorial census, and the 1900 federal census to establish the family in place — then work backward to their state of origin.

quirks: Oklahoma did not become a state until November 16, 1907 — for the Land Run period (1889-1907) the governing jurisdiction was Oklahoma Territory (created May 2, 1890); territorial court, land, and vital records differ in custody from post-statehood records.

Statewide vital registration did not begin at statehood in 1907; the FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Vital Records page returned only generic content — verify the actual start date and level directly with the Oklahoma State Department of Health before assuming any birth or death record exists for this period.

The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire and flood, but an 1890 special territorial census of Oklahoma Territory survives at the Oklahoma Historical Society — a rare exception to the national loss of the 1890 census.

Land Run homestead files (1889-1907) were administered by the General Land Office; land-entry case files are held at NARA (Record Group 49) and partially indexed on FamilySearch and at glorecords.blm.gov. Each file typically includes application, proof of settlement with witnesses, and final patent.
Rejected homestead applications also survive and may contain family details — do not overlook them.

Territorial court records (1890-1907) are split between the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives; naturalization records filed in territorial courts are at those same repositories.

Before the Organic Act of May 2, 1890, the Unassigned Lands were administered without a formal territorial government — records from April 22 to May 2, 1889 (the run itself) are mostly federal land-office documents.
Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other neighboring states — trace origins by searching departure-state records in those jurisdictions as well.

Indian Territory and the Five Civilized Tribes had a parallel record system administered by the Dawes Commission; the Dawes enrollment jackets (1898-1910) are on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 005221389) but are browse-only with 0% name indexing.

Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established new congregations in the newly opened towns — coverage is uneven and many early registers have not been microfilmed or digitized.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory formally created May 2, 1890 (Organic Act), from the Unassigned Lands opened April 22, 1889. Oklahoma became the 46th state November 16, 1907.
- **Administrative centers:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890-1910); Oklahoma City became state capital in 1910.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to May 1890, the Unassigned Lands were administered federally with no formal territorial government. Indian Territory, covering the eastern half of present-day Oklahoma, remained a separate jurisdiction governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under federal oversight until 1907.
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 people entered in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 alone. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional areas. No population tool data was returned for this standardPlace and period.
- **Economy:** Homestead farming, cattle ranching, and early commercial development in new towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Oklahoma City, Norman). Indian Territory had significant agricultural and tribal economies. Oil was discovered near Bartlesville in 1897 and grew rapidly after statehood.
- **Ethnic composition:** The settler population in the Unassigned Lands/Oklahoma Territory was predominantly white American migrants from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states; significant African American communities ("Exodusters" and freedmen); Five Civilized Tribes and other tribal nations in Indian Territory. Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled on the Dawes Rolls.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations established congregations rapidly after 1889. Catholic missions predated settlement in some areas. FamilySearch holds "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images).
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); subsequent land runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission allotment of tribal lands (1893-1906); Oklahoma statehood (November 16, 1907).

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: The Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory (no formal county government). Indian Territory proper — governed by the Five Civilized Tribes — occupied the eastern half of present-day Oklahoma throughout this period.
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory established, initially covering the Unassigned Lands and No Man's Land (the Panhandle). Counties were organized under territorial government.
- 1891-1895: Additional land runs expanded Oklahoma Territory westward and northward as more areas were opened to settlement.
- 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged to form the state of Oklahoma. Records created in Indian Territory before 1907 are held under different federal and tribal custodians than those of Oklahoma Territory.
- **Critical rule:** For any family research, determine whether the ancestor settled in Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory — the record systems are entirely different. A family in the Cherokee Nation (Indian Territory) generated tribal and Dawes Commission records; a family in the Unassigned Lands (Oklahoma Territory) generated federal homestead and territorial court records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Vital Records page returned only generic content rather than Oklahoma-specific information — the exact statewide start date and level cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results. Do not assume statewide birth or death registration existed in the 1889-1907 territorial period. Verify directly with the Oklahoma State Department of Health or the Oklahoma State Archives before assuming a birth/death record exists.
- **What exists (confirmed by tool results):** County marriages from 1890 onward (FamilySearch collection 2134789: "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995," 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images — indexed and searchable by name at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789).
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration dates confirmed by this survey. Territorial-era vital registration was sparse and primarily at the county level if it existed at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, probate records naming heirs, and newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic (missions), and other Protestant denominations established congregations beginning in 1889.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" — covers 123,456 records with 61,728 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Many early registers have not been microfilmed or digitized; check the Oklahoma Historical Society and individual denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.
- **Coverage note:** Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established new congregations; coverage is uneven for the first years after the Land Run.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide — a major gap for Land Run families. The 1900 (full territorial coverage) and 1910 (post-statehood) censuses survive and are name-indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Oklahoma Territory special census (1890):** A rare surviving 1890 special territorial census is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. This is one of the few 1890-era enumerations that survived the 1921 fire and flood that destroyed most of the national 1890 census. This is a critical substitute source for the missing federal 1890 census. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Land Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Indian censuses and rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 — "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" — covers 567,890 records with 283,945 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432). These are essential for families with tribal affiliations or Freedmen status.
- **County tax rolls:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers and can substitute for the missing 1890 federal census. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Territorial Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal public-land state). Oklahoma is a federal-land state — the federal government, not the state, issued the original land grants.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (GLO) administered homestead claims. Settlers filed applications at land offices in Guthrie and Kingfisher (for the 1889 run). The GLO is now the Bureau of Land Management.
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, rejected applications (which also contain family information). Land-entry case files (homestead final proofs) are digitized on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 005221388, 402 images, 74% name-indexed, covering 1889-1907.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office records). Partially indexed on FamilySearch and searchable at the BLM General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). FamilySearch collection 1541872 — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" — covers 234,567 records with 117,283 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872).
- **Important note:** Rejected homestead applications survive and may contain family details — do not overlook them.

### Probate records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** County probate courts were organized as counties were created (from 1890 onward in Oklahoma Territory).
- **Where held:** Oklahoma county courthouses and the Oklahoma State Archives. Territorial-era probate records (1890-1907) are also at the National Archives at Fort Worth. The FamilySearch Catalog and Wiki probate pages returned only generic content; consult the Oklahoma Historical Society or Oklahoma State Archives directly to confirm what has been microfilmed or digitized.

### Court records
- **Types:** Civil and criminal cases, naturalization records, guardianships, name changes. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including territorial district courts.
- **Date range:** Territorial district courts operated 1890-1907; these are the primary courts for the Land Run period.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Territorial Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898) and its aftermath; some Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans. The Indian Wars of the late 1880s also touched the territory.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations, bounty land warrants (Civil War veterans who settled in Oklahoma).
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C. Military records are available through Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous small community and church cemeteries established beginning in 1889. Many are rural with limited documentation.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has coverage for Oklahoma, though rural Land Run-era cemeteries may be incomplete. BillionGraves also has some coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers vary by cemetery; many early cemeteries lacked formal record-keeping. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds some cemetery transcription projects.

### Newspaper records

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1880-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory formally created May 2, 1890 (Organic Act), from the Unassigned Lands opened April 22, 1889. Oklahoma became the 46th state November 16, 1907.
- **Administrative centers:** Guthrie (territorial capital, 1890-1910); Oklahoma City became state capital in 1910.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to May 1890, the Unassigned Lands were administered federally with no formal territorial government. Indian Territory, covering the eastern half of present-day Oklahoma, remained a separate jurisdiction governed by the Five Civilized Tribes under federal oversight until 1907.
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 people entered in the Land Run of April 22, 1889 alone. Subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional areas. No population tool data was returned for this standardPlace and period.
- **Economy:** Homestead farming, cattle ranching, and early commercial development in new towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Oklahoma City, Norman). Indian Territory had significant agricultural and tribal economies. Oil was discovered near Bartlesville in 1897 and grew rapidly after statehood.
- **Ethnic composition:** The settler population in the Unassigned Lands/Oklahoma Territory was predominantly white American migrants from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states; significant African American communities ("Exodusters" and freedmen); Five Civilized Tribes and other tribal nations in Indian Territory. Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes were enrolled on the Dawes Rolls.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and other Protestant denominations established congregations rapidly after 1889. Catholic missions predated settlement in some areas. FamilySearch holds "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records, 61,728 images).
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); subsequent land runs 1891-1895; Dawes Commission allotment of tribal lands (1893-1906); Oklahoma statehood (November 16, 1907).

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: The Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory (no formal county government). Indian Territory proper — governed by the Five Civilized Tribes — occupied the eastern half of present-day Oklahoma throughout this period.
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory established, initially covering the Unassigned Lands and No Man's Land (the Panhandle). Counties were organized under territorial government.
- 1891-1895: Additional land runs expanded Oklahoma Territory westward and northward as more areas were opened to settlement.
- 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged to form the state of Oklahoma. Records created in Indian Territory before 1907 are held under different federal and tribal custodians than those of Oklahoma Territory.
- **Critical rule:** For any family research, determine whether the ancestor settled in Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory — the record systems are entirely different. A family in the Cherokee Nation (Indian Territory) generated tribal and Dawes Commission records; a family in the Unassigned Lands (Oklahoma Territory) generated federal homestead and territorial court records.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Oklahoma Vital Records page returned only generic content rather than Oklahoma-specific information — the exact statewide start date and level cannot be confirmed from this survey's tool results. Do not assume statewide birth or death registration existed in the 1889-1907 territorial period. Verify directly with the Oklahoma State Department of Health or the Oklahoma State Archives before assuming a birth/death record exists.
- **What exists (confirmed by tool results):** County marriages from 1890 onward (FamilySearch collection 2134789: "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995," 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images — indexed and searchable by name at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789).
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration dates confirmed by this survey. Territorial-era vital registration was sparse and primarily at the county level if it existed at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, probate records naming heirs, and newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Catholic (missions), and other Protestant denominations established congregations beginning in 1889.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" — covers 123,456 records with 61,728 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321). Many early registers have not been microfilmed or digitized; check the Oklahoma Historical Society and individual denominational archives.
- **Language:** English.
- **Coverage note:** Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established new congregations; coverage is uneven for the first years after the Land Run.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide — a major gap for Land Run families. The 1900 (full territorial coverage) and 1910 (post-statehood) censuses survive and are name-indexed online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Oklahoma Territory special census (1890):** A rare surviving 1890 special territorial census is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. ## Alabama Before Statehood (~1800): Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Background

The Alabama region around 1800 operated under **layered, overlapping jurisdictions** — not a single authority:

- **Spanish colonial administration at Mobile**, lasting until 1813
- **Mississippi Territory** covering most of the interior from 1798 onward
- **Alabama Territory** (a brief separate territory, 1817–1819)
- **Statehood in 1819**

**Key practical consequence:** No records exist under the name "Alabama" before 1817. For Mobile-area families, no *American* records exist at all before 1813.

---

### Available Record Types

| Record Type | Coverage | FamilySearch Collection | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Land grants** | Territory-wide | BLM General Land Office (free) | Name-indexed, searchable |
| **County marriage bonds** | From ~1809 | Collection 1598408 | Name-indexed with images |
| **Census substitutes** | 1810 | Collection 2016756 | Name-indexed, no images |
| **Church records** | From 1803 | Collection 1986396 | Partially indexed |
| **Civil vital records** | — | — | None exist for this period |

---

### Digitized Browsable Volumes

On your specific question about **browsable digitized image volumes**: the FamilySearch volume search returned **zero digitized image volumes** for Alabama in the 1780–1820 window. This is a significant digitization gap for the pre-statehood period.

---

### Where Physical/Microfilm Records Are Held

- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery — holds the territorial censuses of **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerating Alabama-area settlers (not online)
- **NARA Southeast Regional Facility**, Atlanta — territorial and federal records

---

### Recommended Next Step

The agent suggests narrowing your search by **which part of Alabama** and **which family or question** you are researching, so the right combination of territorial, colonial, and early county records can be targeted in a research plan. The Mobile area (Spanish colonial records) versus the interior (Mississippi Territory records) follow quite different research paths.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region — Pre-Statehood Era (ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood on 14 December 1819. Before that, the present-day area passed through a succession of administrations: French (Mobile, 1702–1763), British West Florida (1763–1780), Spanish Mobile District (1780–1813), Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), and Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single seat. Territorial government for the Mississippi Territory was at Natchez (later Washington, MS). The Mobile district had its own colonial administration.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817); Alabama Territory (1817–1819).
- **Population during period:** No population figure was returned by the population tool for this period. According to Wikipedia, the region saw significant in-migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia following the Creek War of 1813–1814. Mobile was the principal settled town; interior Alabama was sparsely populated by Euro-Americans before 1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, cotton (emerging along river bottoms), river trade via the Mobile and Tombigbee systems.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations in the interior; French Creole and Spanish Creole settlers concentrated at Mobile; Anglo-American settlers arriving from the Carolinas, Virginia, Tennessee, and Georgia after 1800; enslaved African-Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant in Mobile under French and Spanish regimes); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders arriving with Anglo-American settlement after ca. 1800.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile (1702); transfer to Britain (1763); Spanish occupation of Mobile (1780); U.S. annexation of Mobile (1813); Creek War (1813–1814); Alabama Territory organized (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes
- **1702–1763:** Mobile district under France.
- **1763–1780:** Transferred to Britain as part of West Florida.
- **1780–1813:** Spain seized Mobile; the Mobile District operated under Spanish colonial administration.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory established by Congress, covering present-day Mississippi and most of present-day Alabama — but Mobile and its district remained under Spanish control until 1813.
- **1813:** U.S. forces seized Mobile; the Mobile district then fell under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory carved out of the eastern portion of Mississippi Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted to the Union.

**Critical research implication:** Records before 1817 were generated under Mississippi Territory authority (or Spanish/French colonial authority for the Mobile district). There is no single "Alabama" record-keeping chain before statehood. A researcher must work both the Mississippi Territory record trail and the colonial record trail for Mobile concurrently — they are not interchangeable.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil vital registration existed during the 1780–1820 period. The FamilySearch Wiki does not state a statewide registration date for this era. County-level marriage bonds and licenses begin with county formation after ca. 1800 (e.g., the FamilySearch indexed collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" [collection 1598408] begins in 1809). Birth and death registration at the state level came much later in Alabama's history.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses at the county level from county formation onward (earliest in the FamilySearch collection: 1809). No civil birth or death registration for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouses; copies microfilmed by FamilySearch (indexed collection 1598408 covers 1809–1950 with 612,345 records and images).
- **Gaps:** No births or deaths registered civilly. Pre-1809 marriages are not in the FamilySearch indexed collection.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (Catholic sacramental records for Mobile; Baptist and Methodist class records for interior); family Bibles.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, continuous from French settlement ca. 1702); Baptist and Methodist (interior Alabama, arriving with Anglo-American settlement after ca. 1800).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); membership rolls, minutes, conference records (Baptist, Methodist).
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic (Mobile/Spanish era): Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. Earlier French records at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
  - Post-1800 Catholic registers: Diocese of Mobile archives.
  - Baptist and Methodist: Denominational archives; some records microfilmed by FamilySearch. The indexed collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396) covers 156,789 records with partial images, starting 1803.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French and Spanish periods are in French and Spanish respectively.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1800 federal census included Mississippi Territory (which then encompassed present-day Alabama). The 1810 federal census also covers the territory. These are the closest federal enumerations to this period.
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory censuses were taken in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 for settlers in what is now Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Spanish colonial censuses:** Census returns for the Mobile District under Spain are held at the Archivo General de Indias, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch indexed collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, no images) covers from 1810 and serves as an index without images. Pre-1810 territorial censuses are not in this index; they require a visit to ADAH or a written request.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court proceedings.
- **Date range:** County courts organized as counties were created during the territorial period (from ca. 1800 onward for Mississippi Territory counties in the Alabama region).
- **Where held:** County courthouses; the FamilySearch indexed collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764) begins in 1809 and contains 438,210 records with images. Pre-statehood territorial court records are at ADAH and NARA (Record Group 46, Senate territorial papers).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range), applied as U.S. government took title to ceded lands. Colonial-era Spanish and British grants used metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** U.S. General Land Office issued original patents for federal public domain land. Spanish and British colonial grants were issued by colonial governors.
- **Types:** Federal patents (BLM GLO Records, glorecords.blm.gov); Spanish and British colonial grants (Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies); territorial-era tax lists.
- **Date range:** U.S. land office sales in Alabama begin ca. 1803–1806 as Choctaw and Cherokee cessions opened land. Colonial grants predate 1780.
- **Where held:** U.S. patents: BLM GLO website. Colonial grants: Archivo General de Indias (Spanish) / Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (French). Tax lists: ADAH. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast theater); earlier Spanish-era militia service.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (for Creek War veterans), militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files for Creek War / War of 1812); Fold3 (subscription) for digitized service records; ADAH for Alabama militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemetery at Mobile (French/Spanish era); Protestant family and church cemeteries established as Anglo-American settlement expanded after ca. 1800.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcriptions for many Alabama cemeteries but coverage of pre-1820 graves is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for Catholic Mobile cemetery; no centralized burial registry for the territorial period.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (est. 1811) is among the earliest newspapers in the area; very limited survival.
- **Where held:** ADAH; microfilm at the University of Alabama; some digitization at Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices (land sales, estate notices), and political news. Coverage for the pre-1820 period is extremely thin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the principal Gulf Coast port of entry for the Alabama region. New Orleans was also a major entry point for settlers moving upriver.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); naturalization declarations filed in territorial courts; Spanish-era passports and residence permits (Archivo General de Indias).
- **Where held:** NARA for U.S.-era passenger lists; Archivo General de Indias for Spanish-era documentation.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists (property and poll); Spanish-era padrones (tax/census lists).
- **Date range:** Mississippi Territory tax lists from ca. 1800; Spanish padrones from the Mobile District ca. 1780–1813.
- **Where held:** ADAH (territorial lists); Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress (Spanish padrones).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years and can document a man's presence in a county year by year.

### Other record types
- **Militia rolls:** Territorial militia musters list free white male residents; held at ADAH and NARA.
- **Indian trade licenses and treaty records:** Federal records documenting interaction with Creek and Cherokee nations; at NARA and the National Archives Catalog.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century local histories (e.g., Albert James Pickett's *History of Alabama*, 1851) frequently transcribe early records and name founding families.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org) | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950 (collection 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985 (collection 1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810–1890 (collection 2016756, index only, no images); Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950 (collection 1986396) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census collections including 1800 and 1810 Mississippi Territory | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) | Military service records and pension files for Creek War / War of 1812 | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office Records (https://glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama public domain | Free |
| Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) | Digitized historic Alabama newspapers | Free |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Alabama | Free |
| NARA Online Catalog (https://www.archives.gov) | Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory federal records | Free finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey — digitized volumes:** `volume_search` returned 0 digitized volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1820 period. This is a significant digitization gap: pre-statehood territorial materials do not appear to be available as browsable image volumes on FamilySearch for this period. The four FamilySearch indexed collections above begin at 1803–1809 and cover later decades. Materials that do exist for the pre-statehood years are held in physical and microfilm form at ADAH and NARA.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); tax lists; militia rolls; county records | In-person; some online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Southeast Region (Atlanta, GA) | Federal territorial records, land office records, court records | In-person; written request; some digitized at NARA Catalog |
